entries.6857cc431fb1bc511485f2f50e258ddcbd846695: <div sID="gen19369" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="3" osisID="Dan.3" sID="Dan.3"/> <div eID="gen19369" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19370" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19371" type="x-p"/> In the close of the foregoing chapter we left Daniel's companions, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, in honour and power, princes of the provinces, and preferred for their relation to the God of Israel and the interest they had in him. I know not whether I should say. It were well if this honour had all the saints. No, there are many whom it would not be good for; the saints' honour is reserved for another world. But here we have those same three men as much under the king's displeasure as when they were in his favour, and yet more truly, more highly, honoured by their God than there they were honoured by their prince, both by the grace wherewith he enabled them rather to suffer than to sin and by the miraculous and glorious deliverance which he wrought for them out of their sufferings. It is a very memorable story, a glorious instance of the power and goodness of God, and a great encouragement to the constancy of his people in trying times. The apostle refers to it when he mentions, among the believing heroes, those who by faith "quenched the violence of fire," <reference osisRef="Heb.11.34">Heb. xi. 34</reference>. We have here, I. Nebuchadnezzar's erecting and dedicating a golden image, and his requiring all his subjects, of what rank or degree soever, to fall down and worship it, and the general compliance of his people with that command, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.1-Dan.3.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. Information given against the Jewish princes for refusing to worship this golden image, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.8-Dan.3.12">ver. 8-12</reference>. III. Their constant persisting in that refusal, notwithstanding his rage and menaces, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.13-Dan.3.18">ver. 13-18</reference>. IV. The casting of them into the fiery furnace for their refusal, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.19-Dan.3.23">ver. 19-23</reference>. V. Their miraculous preservation in the fire by the power of God, and their invitation out of the fire by the favour of the king, who was by this miracle convinced of his error in casting them in, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.24-Dan.3.27">ver. 24-27</reference>. VI. The honour which the king gave to God hereupon, and the favour he showed to those faithful worthies, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.28-Dan.3.30">ver. 28-30</reference>.
entries.b3ece228fac5b5eff78eaa0f769feb6859b762e6: <div eID="gen19371" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19370" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Nebuchadnezzar's Golden Image. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19372" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold, whose height <hi type="italic">was</hi> threescore cubits, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the breadth thereof six cubits: he set it up in the plain of Dura, in the province of Babylon. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then Nebuchadnezzar the king sent to gather together the princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, to come to the dedication of the image which Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then the princes, the governors, and captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces, were gathered together unto the dedication of the image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up; and they stood before the image that Nebuchadnezzar had set up. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then a herald cried aloud, To you it is commanded, O people, nations, and languages,   5 <hi type="italic">That</hi> at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of music, ye fall down and worship the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king hath set up: <hi type="super">6</hi> And whoso falleth not down and worshippeth shall the same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace. <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore at that time, when all the people heard the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and all kinds of music, all the people, the nations, and the languages, fell down <hi type="italic">and</hi> worshipped the golden image that Nebuchadnezzar the king had set up. <div eID="gen19372" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19373" type="x-p"/> We have no certainty concerning the date of this story, only that if this image, which Nebuchadnezzar dedicated, had any relation to that which he dreamed of, it is probable that it happened not long after that; some reckon it to be about the seventh year of Nebuchadnezzar, a year before Jehoiachin's captivity, in which Ezekiel was carried away. Observe, <div eID="gen19373" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19374" type="x-p"/> I. A <hi type="italic">golden image set up</hi> to be worshipped. Babylon was full of idols already, yet nothing will serve this imperious prince but they must have one more; for those who have forsaken the one only living God, and begin to set up many gods, will find the gods they set up so unsatisfying, and their desire after them so insatiable, that they will multiply them without measure, wander after them endlessly, and never know when they have sufficient. Idolaters are fond of novelty and variety. <hi type="italic">They choose new gods.</hi> Those that have many will wish to have more. Nebuchadnezzar the king, that he might exert the prerogative of his crown, to make what god he thought fit, <hi type="italic">set up</hi> this image, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.1">v. 1</reference>. Observe, 1. The <hi type="italic">valuableness</hi> of it; it was <hi type="italic">an image of gold,</hi> not all gold surely; rich as he was, it is probable that he could not afford that, but overlaid with gold. Note, The worshippers of false gods are not wont to mind charges in setting up images and worshipping them; they <hi type="italic">lavish gold out of the bag</hi> for that purpose (<reference osisRef="Isa.46.6">Isa. xlvi. 6</reference>), which shames our niggardliness in the worship of the true God. 2. The vastness of it; it was <hi type="italic">threescore cubits high and six cubits broad.</hi> It exceeded the ordinary stature of a man fifteen times (for that is reckoned but four cubits, or six feet), as if its being monstrous would make amends for its being lifeless. But why did Nebuchadnezzar set up this image? Some suggest that it was to clear himself from the imputation of having turned a Jew, because he had lately spoken with great honour of the God of Israel and had preferred some of his worshippers. Or perhaps he set it up as an image of himself, and designed to be himself worshipped in it. Proud princes affected to have divine honours paid them; Alexander did so, pretending himself to be the son of Jupiter Olympius. He was told that in the image he had seen in his dream he was represented by the <hi type="italic">head of gold,</hi> which was to be succeeded by kingdoms of baser metal; but here he sets up to be himself the whole image, for he makes it all of gold. See here, (1.) How the good impressions that were then made upon him were quite lost, and quickly. He then acknowledged that the God of Israel is of a truth a <hi type="italic">God of gods</hi> and a <hi type="italic">Lord of kings;</hi> and yet now, in defiance of the express law of that God, he sets up an image to be worshipped, not only continues in his former idolatries, but contrives new ones. Note, Strong convictions often come short of a sound conversion. Many a pang have owned the absurdity and dangerousness of sin, and yet have gone on in it. (2.) How that very dream and the interpretation of it, which then made such good impressions upon him, now had a quite contrary effect. Then it made him fall down as a humble worshipper of God; now it made him set up for a bold competitor with God. Then he thought it a great thing to be the golden head of the image, and owned himself obliged to God for it; but, his mind rising with his condition, now he thinks that too little, and, in contradiction to God himself and his oracle, he will be <hi type="italic">all in all.</hi> <div eID="gen19374" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19375" type="x-p"/> II. A general convention of the states summoned to attend the solemnity of the dedication of this image, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.2-Dan.3.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. Messengers are despatched to all parts of the kingdom to <hi type="italic">gather together the princes,</hi> dukes, and lords, all the peers of the realm, with all officers civil and military, <hi type="italic">the captains</hi> and commanders of the forces, <hi type="italic">the judges, the treasurers or general receivers, the counsellors,</hi> and <hi type="italic">the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces;</hi> they must all <hi type="italic">come to the dedication of this image</hi> upon pain and peril of what shall fall thereon. He summons the great men, for the great honour of his idol; it is therefore mentioned to the glory of Christ that <hi type="italic">kings shall bring presents unto him.</hi> If he can bring them to pay homage to his golden image, he doubts not but the inferior people will follow of course. In obedience to the king's summons all the magistrates and officers of that vast kingdom leave the services of their particular countries, and come to Babylon, to the dedication of this golden image; long journeys many of them took, and expensive ones, upon a very foolish errand; but, as the idols are senseless things, such are the worshippers. <div eID="gen19375" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19376" type="x-p"/> III. A proclamation made, commanding all manner of persons present before the image, upon the signal given, to fall down prostrate, and worship the image, under the style and title of <hi type="italic">The golden image which Nebuchadnezzar the king has set up.</hi> A herald proclaims this aloud throughout this vast assembly of grandees, with their numerous train of servants and attendants, and a great crowd of people, no doubt, that were not sent for; let them all take notice, 1. That the king does strictly charge and command all manner of persons to fall down and <hi type="italic">worship the golden image;</hi> whatever other gods they worship at other times, now they must worship this. 2. That they must all do this just at the same time, in token of their communion with each other in this idolatrous service, and that, in order hereunto, notice shall be given by a concert of music, which would likewise serve to adorn the solemnity and to sweeten and soften the minds of those that were loth to yield and bring them to comply with the king's command. This mirth and gaiety in the worship would be very agreeable to carnal sensual minds, that are strangers to that spiritual worship which is due to God who is a spirit. <div eID="gen19376" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19377" type="x-p"/> IV. The general compliance of the assembly with this command, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.7">v. 7</reference>. They heard the sound of the musical instruments, both wind-instruments and hand-instruments, <hi type="italic">the cornet and flute,</hi> with the <hi type="italic">harp, sackbut, psaltery,</hi> and <hi type="italic">dulcimer,</hi> the melody of which they thought was ravishing (and fit enough it was to excite such a devotion as they were then to pay), and immediately they all, as one man, as soldiers that are wont to be exercised by beat of drum, <hi type="italic">all the people, nations, and languages, fell down and worshipped the golden image.</hi> And no marvel when it was proclaimed, That whosoever would not <hi type="italic">worship this golden image</hi> should be immediately thrown <hi type="italic">into the midst of a burning fiery furnace,</hi> ready prepared for that purpose, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.6">v. 6</reference>. Here were the charms of music to allure them into a compliance and the terrors of the fiery furnace to frighten them into a compliance. Thus beset with temptation, they all yielded. Note, That way that sense directs the most will go; there is nothing so bad which the careless world will not be drawn to by a concert of music, or driven to by a fiery furnace. And by such methods as these false worship has been set up and maintained.
entries.c5e13cb33b1bae801f897b4e7648e3b3b4d39c2a: <div eID="gen19377" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Hebrew Princes Accused; Fortitude of the Jewish Princes. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19378" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Wherefore at that time certain Chaldeans came near, and accused the Jews. <hi type="super">9</hi> They spake and said to the king Nebuchadnezzar, O king, live for ever. <hi type="super">10</hi> Thou, O king, hast made a decree, that every man that shall hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and dulcimer, and all kinds of music, shall fall down and worship the golden image: <hi type="super">11</hi> And whoso falleth not down and worshippeth, <hi type="italic">that</hi> he should be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace. <hi type="super">12</hi> There are certain Jews whom thou hast set over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then Nebuchadnezzar in <hi type="italic">his</hi> rage and fury commanded to bring Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. Then they brought these men before the king. <hi type="super">14</hi> Nebuchadnezzar spake and said unto them, <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> true, O Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, do not ye serve my gods, nor worship the golden image which I have set up? <hi type="super">15</hi> Now if ye be ready that at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, and dulcimer, and all kinds of music, ye fall down and worship the image which I have made; <hi type="italic">well:</hi> but if ye worship not, ye shall be cast the same hour into the midst of a burning fiery furnace; and who <hi type="italic">is</hi> that God that shall deliver you out of my hands? <hi type="super">16</hi> Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, answered and said to the king, O Nebuchadnezzar, we <hi type="italic">are</hi> not careful to answer thee in this matter. <hi type="super">17</hi> If it be <hi type="italic">so,</hi> our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver <hi type="italic">us</hi> out of thine hand, O king. <hi type="super">18</hi> But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up. <div eID="gen19378" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19379" type="x-p"/> It was strange that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, would be present at this assembly, when, it is likely, they knew for what intent it was called together. Daniel, we may suppose, was absent, either his business calling him away or having leave from the king to withdraw, unless we suppose that he stood so high in the king's favour that none durst complain of him for his noncompliance. But why did not his companions keep out of the way? Surely because they would obey the king's orders as far as they could, and would be ready to bear a public testimony against this gross idolatry. They did not think it enough not to bow down to the image, but, being in office, thought themselves obliged to stand up against it, though it was the image which the king their master set up, and would be a golden image to those that worshipped it. Now, <div eID="gen19379" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19380" type="x-p"/> I. Information is brought to the king by <hi type="italic">certain Chaldeans</hi> against these three gentlemen that they did not obey the king's edict, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.8">v. 8</reference>. Perhaps these Chaldeans that accused them were some of those <hi type="italic">magicians or astrologers</hi> that were particularly called <hi type="italic">Chaldeans</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.2">ch. ii. 2, 4</reference>) who bore a grudge to Daniel's companions for his sake, because he had eclipsed them, and so had these companions. They by their prayers had obtained the mercy which saved the lives of these Chaldeans, and, behold, how they requite them evil for good! for their love they are their adversaries. Thus Jeremiah <hi type="italic">stood before God, to speak good for those</hi> who afterwards <hi type="italic">dug a pit for his life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.18.20">Jer. xviii. 20</reference>. We must not think it strange if we meet with such ungrateful men. Or perhaps they were such of the Chaldeans as expected the places to which they were advanced, and envied them their preferments; <hi type="italic">and who can stand before envy ?</hi> They appeal to the king himself concerning the edict, with all due respect to his majesty, and the usual compliment, <hi type="italic">O king! live forever</hi> (as if they aimed at nothing but his honour, and to serve his interest, when really they were putting him upon that which would endanger the ruin of him and his kingdom); they beg leave, 1. To put him in mind of the law he had lately made, That all manner of persons, without exception of nation or language, should <hi type="italic">fall down and worship this golden image;</hi> they put him in mind also of the penalty which by the law was to be inflicted upon recusants, that they were to be <hi type="italic">cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.3.10-Dan.3.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. It cannot be denied but that this was the law; whether a righteous law or no ought to be considered. 2. To inform him that these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, had not conformed to this edict, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">v. 12</reference>. It is probable that Nebuchadnezzar had no particular design to ensnare them in making the law, for then he would himself have had his eye upon them, and would not have needed this information; but their enemies, that sought an occasion against them, laid hold on this, and were forward to accuse them. To aggravate the matter, and incense the king the more against them, (1.) They put him in mind of the dignity to which the criminals had been preferred. Though they were Jews, foreigners, captives, men of a despised nation and religion, yet the king had <hi type="italic">set them over the affairs of the province of Babylon.</hi> It was therefore very ungrateful, and an insufferable piece of insolence, for them to disobey the king's command, when they had shared so much of the king's favour. And, besides, the high station they were in would make their refusal the more scandalous; it would be a bad example, and have a bad influence upon others; and therefore it was necessary that it should be severely animadverted upon. Thus princes that are incensed enough against innocent people commonly have but too many about them who do all they can to make them worse. (2.) They suggest that it was done maliciously, contumaciously, and in contempt of him and his authority: "They have <hi type="italic">set no regard upon thee;</hi> for they <hi type="italic">serve not the gods</hi> which thou servest, and which thou requirest them to serve, nor <hi type="italic">worship the golden image which thou hast set up.</hi>" <div eID="gen19380" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19381" type="x-p"/> II. These three pious Jews are immediately brought before the king, and arraigned and examined upon this information. Nebuchadnezzar fell into a great passion, and <hi type="italic">in his rage and fury commanded</hi> them to be seized, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.13">v. 13</reference>. How little was it the honour of this mighty prince that he had rule over so many nations when at the same time he had no <hi type="italic">rule over his own spirit,</hi> that there were so many who were subjects and captives to him when he was himself a perfect slave to his own brutish passions and led captive by them! How unfit was he to rule reasonable men who could not himself be ruled by reason! It needed not be a surprise to him to hear that these three men did not now serve his gods, for he knew very well they never had served them, and that their religion, which they had always adhered to, forbade them to do it. Nor had he any reason to think that they designed any contempt of his authority, for they had in all instances shown themselves respectful and dutiful to him as their prince. But it was especially unseasonable at this time, when he was in the midst of his devotions, dedicating his golden image, to be in such a rage and fury, and so much to discompose himself. The <hi type="italic">discretion of a man,</hi> one would think, should at least have <hi type="italic">deferred this anger.</hi> True devotion calms the spirit, quiets and meekens it; but superstition, and a devotion to false gods, inflame men's passions, inspire them with rage, and fury, and turn them into brutes. <hi type="italic">The wrath of a king is as the roaring of a lion;</hi> so was the wrath of this king; and yet, when he was in such a heat, these three men were <hi type="italic">brought before him,</hi> and appeared with an undaunted courage, and unshaken constancy. <div eID="gen19381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19382" type="x-p"/> III. The case is laid before them in short, and it is put to them whether they will comply or no. 1. The king asked them whether it was true that they had not worshipped the golden image when others did, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.14">v. 14</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Is it of purpose?</hi>" so some read it. "Was it designedly and deliberately done, or was it only through inadvertency, that you have not <hi type="italic">served my gods?</hi> What! you that I have nourished and brought up, that have been educated and maintained at my charge, that I have been so kind to and done so much for, you that have been in such reputation for wisdom, and therefore should better have known your duty to your prince; what! do not you <hi type="italic">serve my gods nor worship the golden image which I have set up?</hi>" Note, The faithfulness of God's servants to him has often been the wonder of their enemies and persecutors, who <hi type="italic">think it strange</hi> that they <hi type="italic">run not with them to the same excess of riot.</hi> 2. He was willing to admit them to a new trial; if they did on purpose not do it before, yet, it may be, upon second thoughts, they will change their minds; it is therefore repeated to them upon what terms they now stand, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">v. 15</reference>. (1.) The king is willing that music shall play again, only for their sakes, to soften them into a compliance; and if they will not, like the deaf adder, stop their ears, but will hearken to the voice of the charmers and will <hi type="italic">worship the golden image,</hi> well and good; their former omission shall be pardoned. But, (2.) The king is resolved, if they persist in their refusal, that they shall immediately be <hi type="italic">cast into the fiery furnace,</hi> and shall not have so much as an hour's reprieve. Thus does the matter lie in a little compass—<hi type="italic">Turn, or burn;</hi> and, because he knew they buoyed themselves up in their refusal with a confidence in their God, he insolently set him a defiance: "<hi type="italic">And who is that God that shall deliver you out of my hands?</hi> Let him, if he can." Now he forgot what he himself once owned, that their God was a <hi type="italic">God of gods</hi> and a <hi type="italic">Lord of kings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.2.47">ch. ii. 47</reference>. Proud men are still ready to say, as Pharaoh, <hi type="italic">Who is the Lord that I should obey his voice?</hi> or, as Nebuchadnezzar, Who is the Lord, that I should <hi type="italic">fear his power?</hi> <div eID="gen19382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19383" type="x-p"/> IV. They give in their answer, which they all agree in, that they still adhere to their resolution not to worship the golden image, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.16-Dan.3.18">v. 16-18</reference>. We have here such an instance of fortitude and magnanimity as is scarcely to be paralleled. We call these the <hi type="italic">three children</hi> (and they were indeed <hi type="italic">young men</hi>), but we should rather call them the three champions, the <hi type="italic">first three</hi> of the <hi type="italic">worthies</hi> of God's <hi type="italic">kingdom among men.</hi> They did not break out into any intemperate heat or passion against those that did worship the golden image, did not insult or affront them; nor did they rashly thrust themselves upon the trial, or go out of their way to court martyrdom; but, when they were duly called to the fiery trial, they acquitted themselves bravely, with a conduct and courage that became sufferers for so good a cause. The king was not so daringly bad in making this idol, but they were as daringly good in witnessing against it. They keep their temper admirably well, do not call the king a tyrant or an idolater (the cause of God needs not the wrath of man), but, with an exemplary calmness and sedateness of mind, they deliberately give in their answer, which they resolve to abide by. Observe, <div eID="gen19383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19384" type="x-p"/> 1. Their gracious and generous contempt of death, and the noble negligence with which they look upon the dilemma that they are put to: <hi type="italic">O Nebuchadnezzar! we are not careful to answer thee in this matter.</hi> They do not in sullenness deny him an answer, nor stand mute; but they tell him that they are in no care about it. <hi type="italic">There needs not an answer</hi> (so some read it); they are resolved not to comply, and the king is resolved they shall die if they do not; the matter therefore is determined, and why should it be disputed? But it is better read, "<hi type="italic">We want not an answer for thee,</hi> nor have it to seek, but come prepared." (1.) They needed no time to deliberate concerning the matter of their answer; for they did not in the least hesitate whether they should comply or no. It was a matter of life and death, and one would think they might have considered awhile before they had resolved; life is desirable, and death is dreadful. But when the sin and duty that were in the case were immediately determined by the letter of the second commandment, and no room was left to question what was right, the life and death that were in the case were not to be considered. Note, Those that would avoid sin must not parley with temptation. When that which we are allured or affrighted to is manifestly evil the motion is rather to be rejected with indignation and abhorrence than reasoned with; stand not to pause about it, but say, as Christ has taught us, <hi type="italic">Get thee behind me, Satan.</hi> (2.) They needed no time to contrive how they should <hi type="italic">word</hi> it. While they were advocates for God, and were called out to witness in his cause, they doubted not but it should be <hi type="italic">given them in that same hour what they should speak,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.19">Matt. x. 19</reference>. They were not contriving an evasive answer, when a direct answer was expected from them; no, nor would they seem to court the king not to insist upon it. Here is nothing in their answer that looks like compliment; they begin not, as their accusers did, with, <hi type="italic">O king! live for ever,</hi> no artful insinuation, <hi type="italic">ad captandam benevolentiam—to put him into a good humour,</hi> but every thing that is plain and downright: O Nebuchadnezzar! <hi type="italic">we are not careful to answer thee.</hi> Note, Those that make their duty their main care need not be careful concerning the event. <div eID="gen19384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19385" type="x-p"/> 2. Their believing confidence in God and their dependence upon him, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.17">v. 17</reference>. It was this that enabled them to look with so much contempt upon death, death in pomp, death in all its terrors: they trusted in the living God, and by that faith chose rather to suffer than to sin; they therefore <hi type="italic">feared not the wrath of the king,</hi> but endured, because by faith they had an eye to <hi type="italic">him that is invisible</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.25">Heb. xi. 25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.27">27</reference>): "<hi type="italic">If it be so,</hi> if we are brought to this strait, if we must be thrown into the fiery furnace unless we serve thy gods, know then," (1.) "That though we worship not <hi type="italic">thy gods</hi> yet we are not atheists; there is a God whom we can call ours, to whom we faithfully adhere." (2.) "That we serve this God; we have devoted ourselves to his honour; we employ ourselves in his work, and depend upon him to protect us, provide for us, and reward us." (3.) "That we are well assured that this God is <hi type="italic">able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace;</hi> whether he will or no, we are sure that he can either prevent our being cast into the furnace or rescue us out of it." Note, The faithful servants of God will find him a Master able to bear them out in his service, and to control and overrule all the powers that are armed against them. <hi type="italic">Lord, if thou wilt, thou canst.</hi> (4.) "That we have reason to hope <hi type="italic">he will deliver us,</hi>" partly because, in such a vast appearance of idolaters, it would be very much for the honour of his great name to deliver them, and partly because Nebuchadnezzar had defied him to do it—<hi type="italic">Who is that God that shall deliver you?</hi> God sometimes appears wonderfully for the silencing of the blasphemies of the enemy, as well as for the answering of the prayers of his people, <reference osisRef="Ps.74.18-Ps.74.22">Ps. lxxiv. 18-22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.27">Deut. xxxii. 27</reference>. "But, if he do not deliver us from the fiery furnace, he will <hi type="italic">deliver us out of thy hand.</hi>" Nebuchadnezzar can but torment and kill the body, and after that, there is no more that he can do; then they are got out of his reach, delivered out of his hand. Note, Good thoughts of God, and a full assurance that he is with us while we are with him, will help very much to carry us through sufferings; and, if he be for us, we need not fear what man can do unto us; let him do his worst. God will deliver us either from death or in death. <div eID="gen19385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19386" type="x-p"/> 3. Their firm resolution to adhere to their principles, whatever might be the consequence (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">But, if not,</hi> though God should not think fit to deliver us from the fiery furnace (which yet we know he can do), if he should suffer us to <hi type="italic">fall into thy hand,</hi> and fall by thy hand, yet <hi type="italic">be it known unto thee, O king! we will not serve</hi> these gods, though they are <hi type="italic">thy gods, nor worship this golden image,</hi> though thou thyself hast <hi type="italic">set it up.</hi>" They are neither ashamed nor afraid to own their religion, and tell the king to his face that they do not fear him, they will not yield to him; had they consulted with flesh and blood, much might have been said to bring them to a compliance, especially when there was no other way of avoiding death, <hi type="italic">so great a death.</hi> (1.) They were not required to abjure their own God, or to renounce his worship, no, nor by any verbal profession or declaration to own this golden image to be a god, but only to bow down before it, which they might do with a secret reserve of their hearts for the God of Israel, inwardly detesting this idolatry, as Naaman bowed in the house of Rimmon. (2.) They were not to fall into a course of idolatry; it was but one single act that was required of them, which would be done in a minute, and the danger was over, and they might afterwards declare their sorrow for it. (3.) The king that commanded it had an absolute power; they were under it, not only as subjects, but as captives; and, if they did it, it was purely by coercion and duress, which would serve to excuse them. (4.) He had been their benefactor, had educated and preferred them, and in gratitude to him they ought to go as far as they could, though it were to strain a point, a point of conscience. (5.) They were now driven into a strange country, and to those that were so driven out it was, in effect, said, <hi type="italic">Go, and serve other gods,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">1 Sam. xxvi. 19</reference>. It was taken for granted that in their disposition they would <hi type="italic">serve other gods,</hi> and it was made a part of the judgment, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.28">Deut. iv. 28</reference>. They might be excused if they should go down the stream, when it is so strong. (6.) Did not their kings, and their princes, and their fathers, yea, and their priests too, set up idols even in God's temple, and worship them there, and not only bow down to them, but erect altars, burn incense, and offer sacrifices, even their own children, to them? Did not all the ten tribes, for many ages, worship gods of gold at Dan and Bethel? And shall they be more precise than their fathers? <hi type="italic">Communis error facit jus</hi>—<hi type="italic">What all do must be right.</hi> (7.) If they should comply, they would save their lives and keep their places, and so be in a capacity to do a great deal of service to their brethren in Babylon, and to do it long; for they were young men, and rising men. But there is enough in that one word of God wherewith to answer and silence these and many more such like carnal reasonings: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not bow down thyself to any images, nor worship them.</hi> They know they must obey God rather than man; they must rather suffer than sin, and must not do evil that good may come. And therefore none of these things move them; they are resolved rather to die in their integrity than live in their iniquity. While their brethren, who yet remained in their own land, were worshipping images by choice, they in Babylon would not be brought to it by constraint, but, as if they were good by <hi type="italic">antiperistasis,</hi> were most zealous against idolatry in an idolatrous country. And truly, all things considered, the saving of them from this sinful compliance was as great a miracle in the kingdom of grace as the saving of them out of the fiery furnace was in the kingdom of nature. These were those who formerly resolved not to defile themselves with the <hi type="italic">king's meat,</hi> and now they as bravely resolve not to defile themselves with his gods. Note, A stedfast self-denying adherence to God and duty in less instances will qualify and prepare us for the like in greater. And in this we must be resolute, never, under any pretence whatsoever, to worship images, or to say "A confederacy" with those that do so.
entries.13b04350a1fef50881c34f13dee2858da392e268: <div eID="gen19386" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Three Hebrews in the Furnace; Deliverance from the Furnace. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19387" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury, and the form of his visage was changed against Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego: <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> he spake, and commanded that they should heat the furnace one seven times more than it was wont to be heated. <hi type="super">20</hi> And he commanded the most mighty men that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in his army to bind Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to cast <hi type="italic">them</hi> into the burning fiery furnace. <hi type="super">21</hi> Then these men were bound in their coats, their hosen, and their hats, and their <hi type="italic">other</hi> garments, and were cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace. <hi type="super">22</hi> Therefore because the king's commandment was urgent, and the furnace exceeding hot, the flame of the fire slew those men that took up Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego. <hi type="super">23</hi> And these three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, fell down bound into the midst of the burning fiery furnace. <hi type="super">24</hi> Then Nebuchadnezzar the king was astonied, and rose up in haste, <hi type="italic">and</hi> spake, and said unto his counsellors, Did not we cast three men bound into the midst of the fire? They answered and said unto the king, True, O king. <hi type="super">25</hi> He answered and said, Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God. <hi type="super">26</hi> Then Nebuchadnezzar came near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace, <hi type="italic">and</hi> spake, and said, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, ye servants of the most high God, come forth, and come <hi type="italic">hither.</hi> Then Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, came forth of the midst of the fire. <hi type="super">27</hi> And the princes, governors, and captains, and the king's counsellors, being gathered together, saw these men, upon whose bodies the fire had no power, nor was a hair of their head singed, neither were their coats changed, nor the smell of fire had passed on them. <div eID="gen19387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19388" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen19388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19389" type="x-p"/> I. The casting of these three faithful servants of God into the fiery furnace. Nebuchadnezzar had himself known and owned so much of the true God that, one would have thought, though his pride and vanity induced him to make this golden image, and set it up to be worshipped, yet what these young men now said (whom he had formerly found to be wiser than all his wise men) would revive his convictions, and at least engage him to excuse them; but it proved quite otherwise. 1. Instead of being convinced by what they said, he was exasperated, and made more outrageous, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.19">v. 19</reference>. It made him <hi type="italic">full of fury,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">form of his visage was changed</hi> against these men. Note, Brutish passions the more they are indulged the more violent they grow, and even change the countenance, to the great reproach of the wisdom and reason of a man. Nebuchadnezzar, in this heat, exchanged the awful majesty of a prince upon his throne, or a judge upon the bench, for the frightful fury of a <hi type="italic">wild bull in a net.</hi> Would men in a passion but view their faces in a glass, they would blush at their own folly and turn all their displeasure against themselves. 2. Instead of mitigating their punishment, in consideration of their quality and the posts of honour they were in, he ordered it to be heightened, that they should <hi type="italic">heat the furnace seven times more than it was wont to be heated</hi> for other malefactors, that is, that they should put seven times more fuel to it, which, though it would not make their death more grievous, but rather dispatch them sooner, was designed to signify that the king looked upon their crime as seven times more heinous than the crimes of others, and so made their death more ignominious. But God brought glory to himself out of this foolish instance of the tyrant's rage; for, though it would not have made their death the more grievous, yet it did make their deliverance much the more illustrious. 3. He ordered them to be bound in their clothes, and cast into the midst of the burning fiery furnace, which was done accordingly, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.20-Dan.3.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. They were bound, that they might not struggle, or make any resistance, were bound in their clothes, for haste, or that they might be consumed the more slowly and gradually. But God's providence ordered it for the increase of the miracle, in that their clothes were not so much as singed. They were bound in their <hi type="italic">coats</hi> or mantles, their <hi type="italic">hosen</hi> or breeches, and their <hi type="italic">hats</hi> or turbans, as if, in detestation of their crime, they would have their clothes to be burnt with them. What a terrible death was this—to be <hi type="italic">cast bound into the midst of a burning fiery furnace!</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.3.23">v. 23</reference>. It makes one's flesh tremble to think of it, and horror to take hold on one. It is amazing that the tyrant was so hard-hearted as to inflict such a punishment, and that the confessors were so stout-hearted as to submit to it rather than sin against God. But what is this to the <hi type="italic">second death,</hi> to that furnace into which the tares shall be cast in bundles, to that lake which burns eternally with fire and brimstone? Let Nebuchadnezzar heat his furnace as hot as he can, a few minutes will finish the torment of those who are cast into it; but hell-fire tortures and does not kill. The pain of damned sinners is more exquisite, and the <hi type="italic">smoke of their torment ascends for ever and ever,</hi> and <hi type="italic">those have no rest,</hi> no intermission, no cessation of their pains, <hi type="italic">who have worshipped the beast and his image</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.10-Rev.14.11">Rev. xiv. 10, 11</reference>), whereas their pain would be soon over that were cast into this furnace for not worshipping this Babylonian beast and his image. 4. It was a remarkable providence that the men, the <hi type="italic">mighty men,</hi> that bound them, and threw them into the furnace, were themselves consumed or suffocated by the flame, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.22">v. 22</reference>. The <hi type="italic">king's commandment was urgent,</hi> that they should dispatch them quickly, and be sure to do it effectually; and therefore they resolved to go to the very mouth of the furnace, that they might throw them <hi type="italic">into the midst</hi> of it, but they were in such haste that they would not take time to arm themselves accordingly. The apocryphal additions to Daniel say that the flame ascended forty-nine cubits above the mouth of the furnace. Probably God ordered it so that the wind blew it directly upon them with such violence that it smothered them. God did thus immediately plead the cause of his injured servants, and take vengeance for them on their persecutors, whom he punished, not only in the very act of their sin, but by it. But these men were only the instruments of cruelty; he that bade them do it had the greater sin; yet they suffered justly for executing an unjust decree, and it is very probable that they did it with pleasure and were glad to be so employed. Nebuchadnezzar himself was reserved for a further reckoning. There is a day coming when proud tyrants will be punished, not only for the cruelties they have been guilty of, but for employing those about them in their cruelties, and so exposing them to the judgments of God. <div eID="gen19389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19390" type="x-p"/> II. The deliverance of these three faithful servants of God out of the furnace. When they were cast bound into the midst of that devouring fire we might well conclude that we should hear no more of them, that their very bones would be calcined; but, to our amazement, we here find that Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, are yet alive. <div eID="gen19390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19391" type="x-p"/> 1. Nebuchadnezzar finds them walking in the fire. <hi type="italic">He was astonished, and rose up in haste,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.3.24">v. 24</reference>. Perhaps the slaying of the men that executed his sentence was that which astonished him, as well it might, for he had reason to think his own turn would be next; or it was some unaccountable impression upon his own mind that astonished him, and made him rise up in haste, and go to the furnace, to see what had become of those he had cast into it. Note, God can strike those with astonishment whose hearts are most hardened both against him and against his people. He that made the soul can make his sword to approach to it, even to that of the greatest tyrant. In his astonishment he calls his counsellors about him, and appeals to them. <hi type="italic">Did we not cast three men bound into the fire?</hi> It seems, it was done by order, not only of the king, but of the council. They durst not but concur with him, which he forced them to do, that they might share with him in the guilt and odium? "<hi type="italic">True, O king!</hi>" say they; "we did order such an execution to be done and it was done." "But now," says the king, "I have been looking into the furnace, and I <hi type="italic">see four men, loose, walking in the midst of the fire,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Dan.3.25">v. 25</reference>. (1.) They were loosed from their bonds. The fire that did not so much as singe their clothes burnt the cords wherewith they were bound, and set them at liberty; thus God's people have their hearts enlarged, through the grace of God, by those very troubles with which their enemies designed to straiten and hamper them. (2.) They had no hurt, made no complaint, felt no pain or uneasiness in the least; the flame did not scorch them; the smoke did not stifle them; they were alive and as well as ever in the midst of the flames. See how God of nature can, when he pleases, control the powers of nature, to make them serve his purposes. Now was fulfilled in the letter gracious promise (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.2">Isa. xliii. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">When thou walkest through the fire thou shalt not be burnt, neither shall the flame kindle upon thee.</hi> By faith they <hi type="italic">quench the violence of the fire, quench the fiery darts of the wicked.</hi> (3.) They <hi type="italic">walked in the midst of the fire.</hi> The furnace was large, so that they had room to walk; they were unhurt, so that they were able to walk; their minds were easy, so that they were disposed to walk, as in a paradise or garden of pleasure. <hi type="italic">Can a man walk upon hot coals and his feet not be burnt?</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.6.28">Prov. vi. 28</reference>. Yes, they did it with as much pleasure as the king of Tyrus <hi type="italic">walked up and down in the midst of his stones of fire,</hi> his precious stones that sparkled as fire, <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.14">Ezek. xxviii. 14</reference>. They were not striving to get out, finding themselves unhurt; but, leaving it to that God who preserved them in the fire to bring them out of it, they walked up and down <hi type="italic">in the midst of it</hi> unconcerned. One of the apocryphal writings relates at large the prayer which Azariah, one of the three, prayed in the fire (wherein he laments the calamities and iniquities of Israel, and entreats God's favour to his people), and the song of praise which they all three sang in the midst of the flames, in both which there are remarkable strains of devotion; but we have reason to think, with Grotius, that they were composed by some Jew of a later age, not as what were used, but only as what might have been used, on this occasion, and therefore we justly reject them as no part of holy writ. (4.) There was a fourth seen with them in the fire, whose form, in Nebuchadnezzar's judgment, was <hi type="italic">like the Son of God;</hi> he appeared as a divine person, a messenger from heaven, not as a servant, but as a son. <hi type="italic">Like an angel</hi> (so some); and angels are called <hi type="italic">sons of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.38.7">Job xxxviii. 7</reference>. In the apocryphal narrative of this story it is said, <hi type="italic">The angel of the Lord came down into the furnace;</hi> and Nebuchadnezzar here says (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">v. 28</reference>), God <hi type="italic">sent his angel and delivered them;</hi> and it was an angel that shut the lions' mouths when Daniel was in the den, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.22">ch. vi. 22</reference>. But some think it was the eternal Son of God, the angel of the covenant, and not a created angel. He appeared often in our nature before he assumed it in his incarnation, and never more seasonable, nor to give a more proper indication and presage of his great errand into the world in the fulness of time, than now, when, to deliver his chosen out of the fire, he came and walked with them in the fire. Note, Those that suffer for Christ have his gracious presence with them in their sufferings, even in the fiery furnace, even in the valley of the shadow of death, and therefore even there they need <hi type="italic">fear no evil.</hi> Hereby Christ showed that what is done against his people he takes as done against himself; whoever throws them into the furnace does, in effect, throw him in. <hi type="italic">I am Jesus, whom thou persecutest,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Isa. lxiii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen19391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19392" type="x-p"/> 2. Nebuchadnezzar calls them out of the furnace (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.26">v. 26</reference>): He <hi type="italic">comes near to the mouth of the burning fiery furnace,</hi> and bids them <hi type="italic">come forth and come hither. Come forth, come</hi> (so some read it); he speaks with a great deal of tenderness and concern, and stands ready to lend them his hand and help them out. He is convinced by their miraculous preservation that he did evil in casting them into the furnace; and therefore he does not <hi type="italic">thrust them out privily; no verily, but he will come himself and fetch them out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.16.37">Acts xvi. 37</reference>. Observe the respectful title that he gives them. When he was in the heat of his fury and rage against them it is probable that he called them rebels, and traitors, and all the ill names he could invent; but now he owns them <hi type="italic">for the servants of the most high God,</hi> a God who now appears <hi type="italic">able to deliver them out of his hand.</hi> Note, Sooner or later, God will convince the proudest of men that he is the most high God, and above them, and too hard for them, even in those things wherein they deal proudly and presumptuously, <reference osisRef="Exod.18.11">Exod. xviii. 11</reference>. He will likewise let them know are who his servants, and that he owns them and will stand by them. Elijah prayed (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.36">1 Kings xviii. 36</reference>), <hi type="italic">Let it be known that thou art God and that I am thy servant.</hi> Nebuchadnezzar now embraces those whom he had abandoned, and is very officious about them, now that he perceives them to be the favourites of Heaven. Note, What persecutors have done against God's servants, when God opens their eyes, they must as far as they can undo again. How the <hi type="italic">fourth,</hi> whose <hi type="italic">form was like the Son of God,</hi> withdrew, and whether he vanished away or visibly ascended, we are not told, but of the other three we are informed, (1.) That they <hi type="italic">came forth out of the midst of the fire,</hi> as Abraham their father out of Ur (that is, <hi type="italic">the fire) of the Chaldees,</hi> into which, says this tradition of the Jews, he was cast, for refusing to worship idols, and out of which he was delivered, as those his <hi type="italic">three children</hi> were. When they had their discharge they did not tempt God by staying in any longer, but came forth as brands out of the burning. (2.) That it was made to appear, to the full satisfaction of all the amazed spectators, that they had not received the least damage by the fire, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.27">v. 27</reference>. All the great men came together to view them, and found that there was not so much as <hi type="italic">a hair of their head singed.</hi> Here that was true in the letter which our Saviour spoke figuratively, for an assurance to his suffering servants that they should sustain no real damage (<reference osisRef="Luke.21.18">Luke xxi. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">There shall not a hair of your head perish.</hi> Their clothes did not so much as change colour, nor smell of fire, much less were their bodies in the least scorched or blistered; no, <hi type="italic">the fire had no power on them.</hi> The Chaldeans worshipped the fire, as a sort of image of the sun, so that, in restraining the fire now, God put contempt, not only upon their king, but upon their god too, and showed that <hi type="italic">his voice divides the flames of fire</hi> as well as the floods of water (<reference osisRef="Ps.29.7">Ps. xxix. 7</reference>), when he pleases to make a way for his people through the midst of it. It is our God only that is <hi type="italic">the consuming fire</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.29">Heb. xii. 29</reference>); other fire, if he but speak the word, shall not consume.
entries.9d45b5f1dec263e86c12b2a79cc39e434c19d82c: <div eID="gen19392" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Nebuchadnezzar Gives Glory to God; Nebuchadnezzar Honours God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 587.)</title> <div sID="gen19393" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">28</hi> <hi type="italic">Then</hi> Nebuchadnezzar spake, and said, Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, who hath sent his angel, and delivered his servants that trusted in him, and have changed the king's word, and yielded their bodies, that they might not serve nor worship any god, except their own God. <hi type="super">29</hi> Therefore I make a decree, That every people, nation, and language, which speak any thing amiss against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, shall be cut in pieces, and their houses shall be made a dunghill: because there is no other God that can deliver after this sort. <hi type="super">30</hi> Then the king promoted Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, in the province of Babylon. <div eID="gen19393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19394" type="x-p"/> The strict observations that were made, <hi type="italic">super visum corporis—on inspecting their bodies,</hi> by the princes and governors, and all the great men who were present upon this public occasion, and who could not be supposed partial in favour of the confessors, contributed much to the clearing of this miracle and the magnifying of the power and grace of God in it. <hi type="italic">That indeed a notable miracle has been done is manifest, and we cannot deny it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.4.16">Acts iv. 16</reference>. Let us now see what effect it had upon Nebuchadnezzar. <div eID="gen19394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19395" type="x-p"/> I. He gives glory to the God of Israel as a God able and ready to protect his worshippers (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">v. 28</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Blessed be the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.</hi> Let him have the honour both of the faithful allegiance which his subjects bear to him and the powerful protection he grants to them, neither of which can be paralleled by any other nation and their gods." The king does himself acknowledge and adore him, and thinks it is fit that he should be acknowledged and adored by all. <hi type="italic">Blessed be thee God of Shadrach.</hi> Note, God can extort confessions of his blessedness even from those that have been ready to curse him to his face. 1. He gives him the glory of his power, that he was able to protect his worshippers against the most mighty and malign ant enemies: <hi type="italic">There is no other God that can deliver after this sort</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.29">v. 29</reference>), no, not this golden image which he had set up. For this reason there was no other god that obliged his worshippers to cleave to him only, and to suffer death rather than worship any other, as the God of Israel did, for they could not engage to bear them out in so doing, as he could. If God can work such deliverance as no other can, he may demand such obedience as no other may. 2. He gives him the glory of his goodness, that he was ready to do it (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">He has sent his angel and delivered his servants.</hi> Bel could not save his worshippers from being burnt at the mouth of the furnace, but the God of Israel saved his from being burnt when they were cast into the midst of the furnace because they refused to <hi type="italic">worship any other god.</hi> By this Nebuchadnezzar was plainly given to understand that all the great success which he had had, and should yet have, against the people of Israel, which he gloried in, as he had therein overpowered the God of Israel, was owing purely <hi type="italic">to their sin:</hi> if the body of that nation had faithfully adhered to their own God and the worship of him only, as these three men did, they would all have been delivered out of his hand as these three men were. And this was a necessary instruction for him at this time. <div eID="gen19395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19396" type="x-p"/> II. He applauds the constancy of these three men in their religion, and describes it to their honour, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">v. 28</reference>. Though he is not himself persuaded to own their God for his and to worship him, because, if he do so, he knows he must worship him only and renounce all others, and he calls him <hi type="italic">the God of Shadrach,</hi> not <hi type="italic">my</hi> God, yet he commends them for cleaving to him, and <hi type="italic">not serving nor worshipping any other God but their own.</hi> Note, There are many who are not religious themselves, and yet will own that those are clearly in the right that are religious and are stedfast in their religion. Though they are not themselves persuaded to close with it, they will commend those who, having closed with it, cleave to it. If men have given up their names to that God who will alone be served, let them keep to their principles, and serve him only, whatever it cost them. Such a constancy in the true religion will turn to men's praise, even among those that are without, when unsteadiness, treachery, and double dealing, are what all men will cry shame on. He commends them that they did this, 1. With a generous contempt of their lives, which they valued not, in comparison with the favour of God and the testimony of a good conscience. They <hi type="italic">yielded their</hi> own <hi type="italic">bodies</hi> to be cast into the fiery furnace rather than they would not only not forsake their God, but not affront him, by once paying that homage to any other which is due to him alone. Note, Those shall have their praise, if not of men, yet of God, who prefer their souls before their bodies, and will rather lose their lives than forsake their God. Those know not the worth and value of religion who do not think it worth suffering for. 2. They did it with a glorious contradiction to their prince: They <hi type="italic">changed the king's word,</hi> that is, they were contrary to it, and thereby put contempt upon both his precepts and threatenings, and made him repent and revoke both. Note, Even kings themselves must own that, when their commands are contrary to the commands of God, he is to be obeyed and not they. (3.) They did it with a gracious confidence in their God. They <hi type="italic">trusted in him</hi> that he would stand by them in what they did, that he would either bring them out of the fiery furnace back to their place on earth or lead them through the fiery furnace forward to their place in heaven; and in this confidence they became fearless of the king's wrath and regardless of their own lives. Note, A stedfast faith in God will produce a stedfast faithfulness to God. Now this honourable testimony, thus publicly borne by the king himself to these servants of God, we may well think, would have a good influence upon the rest of the Jews that were, or should be, captives in Babylon. Their neighbours could not with any confidence urge them to do that, nor could they for shame do that, which their brethren were so highly applauded by the king himself for not doing. Nay, and what God did for these his servants would help not only to keep the Jews close to their religion while they were in captivity, but to cure them of their inclination to idolatry, for which end they were sent into captivity; and, when it had had that blessed effect upon them, they might be assured that God would deliver them out of that furnace, as now he delivered their brethren out of this. <div eID="gen19396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19397" type="x-p"/> III. He issues a royal edict, strictly forbidding any to speak evil of the God of Israel, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.29">v. 29</reference>. We have reason to think that both the sins and the troubles of Israel had given great occasion, though no just occasion, to the Chaldeans to blaspheme the God of Israel, and, it is likely, Nebuchadnezzar himself had encouraged it; but now, though he is no true convert, nor is wrought upon to worship him, yet he resolves never to speak ill of him again, nor to suffer others to do so: "<hi type="italic">Whoever shall speak any thing amiss,</hi> any <hi type="italic">error</hi> (so some), or rather any reproach or blasphemy, whoever shall speak with contempt of <hi type="italic">the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego,</hi> they shall be counted the worst of malefactors, and dealt with accordingly, they shall be <hi type="italic">cut in pieces,</hi> as Agag was by the sword of Samuel, and their houses shall be demolished and made a <hi type="italic">dunghill.</hi>" The miracle now wrought by the power of this God in defence of his worshippers, publicly in the sight of the thousands of Babylon, was a sufficient justification of this edict. And it would contribute much to the ease of the Jews in their captivity to be by this law screened from the fiery darts of reproach and blasphemy, with which otherwise they would have been continually annoyed. Note, It is a great mercy to the church, and a good point gained, when its enemies though they have not their hearts turned, yet have their mouths stopped and their tongues tied. If a heathen prince laid such a restraint upon the proud lips of blasphemers, much more should Christian princes do it; nay, in this thing, one would think that men should be a law to themselves, and that those who have so little love to God that they care not to speak well of him, yet could never find in their hearts, for we are sure they could never find cause, to <hi type="italic">speak any thing amiss</hi> of him. <div eID="gen19397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19398" type="x-p"/> IV. He not only reverses the attainder of these three men, but restores them to their places in the government (<hi type="italic">makes them to prosper,</hi> so the word is), and prefers them to greater and more advantageous trusts than they had been in before: He <hi type="italic">promoted them in the province</hi> of Babylon, which was much to their honour and the comfort of their brethren in captivity there. Note, It is the wisdom of princes to prefer and employ men of stedfastness in religion; for those are most likely to be faithful to them who are faithful to God, and it is likely to be well with them when God's favourites are made theirs.  <chapter eID="Dan.3"/> <div eID="gen19398" type="x-p"/>

entries.e1dd50fb43d01d7044e7c1bd93e9f0580834b52d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11985"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 3</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Dan.3.1-Dan.3.30">Da 3:1-30</reference>. Nebuchadnezzar's Idolatrous Image; Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego Are Delivered from the Furnace.</title> <div sID="gen21662" type="x-p"/> Between the vision of Nebuchadnezzar in the second chapter and that of Daniel in the seventh, four narratives of Daniel's and his friends' personal history are introduced. As the second and seventh chapters go together, so the third and sixth chapters (the deliverance from the lions' den), and the fourth and fifth chapters. Of these last two pairs, the former shows God's nearness to save His saints when faithful to Him, at the very time they seem to be crushed by the world power. The second pair shows, in the case of the two kings of the first monarchy, how God can suddenly humble the world power in the height of its insolence. The latter advances from mere self-glorification, in the fourth chapter, to open opposition to God in the fifth. Nebuchadnezzar demands homage to be paid to his image (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.1-Dan.3.6">Da 3:1-6</reference>), and boasts of his power (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.1-Dan.4.18">Da 4:1-18</reference>). But Belshazzar goes further, blaspheming God by polluting His holy vessels. There is a similar progression in the conduct of God's people. Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego refuse positive homage to the image of the world power (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">Da 3:12</reference>); Daniel will not yield it even a negative homage, by omitting for a time the worship of God (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.10">Da 6:10</reference>). Jehovah's power manifested for the saints against the world in individual histories (the third through sixth chapters) is exhibited in the second and seventh chapters, in world-wide prophetical pictures; the former heightening the effect of the latter. The miracles wrought in behalf of Daniel and his friends were a manifestation of God's glory in Daniel's person, as the representative of the theocracy before the Babylonian king, who deemed himself almighty, at a time when God could not manifest it in His people as a body. They tended also to secure, by their impressive character, that respect for the covenant-people on the part of the heathen powers which issued in Cyrus' decree, not only restoring the Jews, but ascribing honor to the God of heaven, and commanding the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.1-Ezra.1.4">Ezr 1:1-4</reference>) [Auberlen].<div eID="gen21662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11985"/><hi type="bold">1. image--</hi>Nebuchadnezzar's confession of God did not prevent him being a worshipper of idols, besides. Ancient idolaters thought that each nation had its own gods, and that, in addition to these, foreign gods might be worshipped. The Jewish religion was the only exclusive one that claimed all homage for Jehovah as the only true God. Men will in times of trouble confess God, if they are allowed to retain their favorite heart-idols. The image was that of Bel, the Babylonian tutelary god; or rather, Nebuchadnezzar himself, the personification and representative of the Babylonian empire, as suggested to him by the dream (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.38">Da 2:38</reference>), "Thou art this head of gold." The interval between the dream and the event here was about nineteen years. Nebuchadnezzar had just returned from finishing the Jewish and Syrian wars, the spoils of which would furnish the means of rearing such a colossal statue [Prideaux]. The colossal size makes it likely that the frame was wood, overlaid with gold. The "height," sixty cubits, is so out of proportion with the "breadth," exceeding it ten times, that it seems best to suppose the thickness from breast to back to be intended, which is exactly the right proportion of a well-formed man [Augustine, The City of God, 15.26]. Prideaux thinks the sixty cubits refer to the image and pedestal together, the image being twenty-seven cubits high, or forty feet, the pedestal thirty-three cubits, or fifty feet. Herodotus [1.183] confirms this by mentioning a similar image, forty feet high, in the temple of Belus at Babylon. It was not the same image, for the one here was on the plain of Dura, not in the city. <div eID="gen21663" type="x-p"/>
entries.be33bca97e983ceb297231abf6ef4261b7c7727f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11986"/><div sID="gen21664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11986"/><hi type="bold">2. princes--</hi>"satraps" of provinces [Gesenius].<div eID="gen21664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21665" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">captains--</hi>rulers, not exclusively military.<div eID="gen21665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sheriffs--</hi>men learned in the law, like the Arab mufti [Gesenius]. <div eID="gen21666" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d28f10c80cab91a3f25ed471a3c97163fe0ca0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11987"/><div sID="gen21667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11987"/><hi type="bold">3. stood before the image--</hi>in an attitude of devotion. Whatever the king approved of, they all approve of. There is no stability of principle in the ungodly. <div eID="gen21667" type="x-p"/>
entries.44b88909bff00b77684335d1e8b987474000fe58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11988"/><div sID="gen21668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11988"/>4. The arguments of the persecutor are in brief, Turn or burn. <div eID="gen21668" type="x-p"/>
entries.d016845780ac5c7fc71819348a459630d0f83cb8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11989"/><div sID="gen21669" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11989"/><hi type="bold">5. cornet--</hi>A wind instrument, like the French horn, is meant.<div eID="gen21669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21670" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flute--</hi>a pipe or pipes, not blown transversely as our "flute," but by mouthpieces at the end.<div eID="gen21670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sackbut--</hi>a triangular stringed instrument, having short strings, the sound being on a high sharp key.<div eID="gen21671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21672" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">psaltery--</hi>a kind of harp.<div eID="gen21672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21673" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dulcimer--</hi>a bagpipe consisting of two pipes, thrust through a leathern bag, emitting a sweet plaintive sound. Chaldee sumponya, the modern Italian zampogna, Asiatic zambonja.<div eID="gen21673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fall down--</hi>that the recusants might be the more readily detected. <div eID="gen21674" type="x-p"/>
entries.f4a2e97b5a860703f8798d3f0f5aa8a3994bb4d2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11990"/><div sID="gen21675" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11990"/>6. No other nation but the Jews would feel this edict oppressive; for it did not prevent them worshipping their own gods besides. It was evidently aimed at the Jews by those jealous of their high position in the king's court, who therefore induced the king to pass an edict as to all recusants, representing such refusal of homage as an act of treason to Nebuchadnezzar as civil and religious "head" of the empire. So the edict under Darius (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.7-Dan.6.9">Da 6:7-9</reference>) was aimed against the Jews by those jealous of Daniel's influence. The literal image of Nebuchadnezzar is a typical prophecy of "the image of the beast," connected with mystical Babylon, in <reference osisRef="Rev.13.14">Re 13:14</reference>. The second mystical beast there causeth the earth, and them that dwell therein, to worship the first beast, and that as many as would not, should be killed (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.12">Re 13:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.13.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen21675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21676" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">furnace--</hi>a common mode of punishment in Babylon (<reference osisRef="Jer.29.22">Jr 29:22</reference>). It is not necessary to suppose that the furnace was made for the occasion. Compare "brick-kiln," <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.31">2Sa 12:31</reference>. Any furnace for common purposes in the vicinity of Dura would serve. Chardin, in his travels (A.D. 1671-1677), mentions that in Persia, to terrify those who took advantage of scarcity to sell provisions at exorbitant prices, the cooks were roasted over a slow fire, and the bakers cast into a burning oven. <div eID="gen21676" type="x-p"/>
entries.f733dc8a5a20a32b0a490771706e4df1c580e5f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11991"/><div sID="gen21677" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11991"/>7. None of the Jews seem to have been present, except the officers, summoned specially. <div eID="gen21677" type="x-p"/>
entries.d17706167fc603ea6a1ca1ec8f6d00f7ee5b45ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11992"/><div sID="gen21678" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11992"/><hi type="bold">8. accused the Jews--</hi>literally, "ate the rent limbs," or flesh of the Jews (compare <reference osisRef="Job.31.31">Job 31:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.14.4">Psa 14:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.2">27:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">Jr 10:25</reference>). Not probably in general, but as <reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">Da 3:12</reference> states, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego. Why Daniel was not summoned does not appear. Probably he was in some distant part of the empire on state business, and the general summons (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.2">Da 3:2</reference>) had not time to reach him before the dedication. Also, the Jews' enemies found it more politic to begin by attacking Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, who were nearer at hand, and had less influence, before they proceeded to attack Daniel. <div eID="gen21678" type="x-p"/>
entries.d61035046cd601eda1fadd55c54abe50b17b2b09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11993"/><div sID="gen21679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11993"/><hi type="bold">9. live for ever--</hi>A preface of flattery is closely akin to the cruelty that follows. So <reference osisRef="Acts.24.2">Ac 24:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.24.3">3</reference>, &c., Tertullus in accusing Paul before Felix. <div eID="gen21679" type="x-p"/>
entries.0e31236ecc6b08fb73b92cdd0159681c20312236: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11994"/><div sID="gen21680" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11994"/><hi type="bold">12. serve not thy gods--</hi>not only not the golden image, but also not any of Nebuchadnezzar's gods. <div eID="gen21680" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9e247e37b0ab9e6d9b93f28c7317c0322bba358: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11995"/><div sID="gen21681" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11995"/><hi type="bold">13. bring--</hi>Instead of commanding their immediate execution, as in the case of the Magi (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.12">Da 2:12</reference>), Providence inclined him to command the recusants to be brought before him, so that their noble "testimony" for God might be given before the world powers "against them" (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.18">Mt 10:18</reference>), to the edification of the Church in all ages. <div eID="gen21681" type="x-p"/>
entries.26f26ade2feb370b9832a8bf5b27f15fc9fe77f7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11996"/><div sID="gen21682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11996"/><hi type="bold">14. Is it true--</hi>rather, as the Margin [Theodotion], "Is it purposely that?" &c. Compare the Hebrew, <reference osisRef="Num.35.20">Nu 35:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.35.22">22</reference>. Notwithstanding his "fury," his past favor for them disposes him to give them the opportunity of excusing themselves on the ground that their disobedience had not been intentional; so he gives them another trial to see whether they would still worship the image. <div eID="gen21682" type="x-p"/>
entries.740dbe7dc42017b53d198a506776a635815d3bc3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11997"/><div sID="gen21683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11997"/><hi type="bold">15. who is that God--</hi>so Sennacherib's taunt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.35">2Ki 18:35</reference>), and Pharaoh's (<reference osisRef="Exod.5.2">Ex 5:2</reference>). <div eID="gen21683" type="x-p"/>
entries.3cd7eed4692bc169db4121861deb2d27e732bb3c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11998"/><div sID="gen21684" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11998"/><hi type="bold">16. not careful to answer thee--</hi>rather, "We have no need to answer thee"; thou art determined on thy side, and our mind is made up not to worship the image: there is therefore no use in our arguing as if we could be shaken from our principles. Hesitation, or parleying with sin, is fatal; unhesitating decision is the only safety, where the path of duty is clear (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.19">Mt 10:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.28">28</reference>). <div eID="gen21684" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ba0310f4f83097cbc6bf7820966c7543e90974f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv11999"/><div sID="gen21685" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv11999"/><hi type="bold">17. If it be so--</hi>Vatablus translates, "Assuredly." English Version agrees better with the original. The sense is, If it be our lot to be cast into the furnace, our God (quoted from <reference osisRef="Deut.6.4">De 6:4</reference>) is able to deliver us (a reply to Nebuchadnezzar's challenge, "Who is that God that shall deliver you?"); and He will deliver us (either from death, or in death, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.17">2Ti 4:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.18">18</reference>). He will, we trust, literally deliver us, but certainly He will do so spiritually. <div eID="gen21685" type="x-p"/>
entries.a5d933146a40b712bd318ed8ffeea302aa1ce112: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12000"/><div sID="gen21686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12000"/><hi type="bold">18. But if not, &c.--</hi>connected with <reference osisRef="Dan.3.18">Da 3:18</reference>. "Whether our God deliver us, as He is able, or do not, we will not serve thy gods." Their service of God is not mercenary in its motive. Though He slay them, they will still trust in Him (<reference osisRef="Job.13.15">Job 13:15</reference>). Their deliverance from sinful compliance was as great a miracle in the kingdom of grace, as that from the furnace was in the kingdom of nature. Their youth, and position as captives and friendless exiles, before the absolute world potentate and the horrid death awaiting them if they should persevere in their faith, all enhance the grace of God, which carried them through such an ordeal. <div eID="gen21686" type="x-p"/>
