entries.04dc395885db390a254d925897ba34b2971481c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12001"/><div sID="gen21687" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12001"/><hi type="bold">19. visage ... changed--</hi>He had shown forbearance (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.14">Da 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">15</reference>) as a favor to them, but now that they despise even his forbearance, anger "fills" him, and is betrayed in his whole countenance.<div eID="gen21687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21688" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seven times more than it was wont--</hi>literally, "than it was (ever) seen to be heated." Seven is the perfect number; that is, it was made as hot as possible. Passion overdoes and defeats its own end, for the hotter the fire, the sooner were they likely to be put out of pain. <div eID="gen21688" type="x-p"/>
entries.4471f043165be24925596802452360a9859e627c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12002"/><div sID="gen21689" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12002"/><hi type="bold">21. coats ... hosen ... hats--</hi>Herodotus [1.195] says that the Babylonian costume consisted of three parts: (1) wide, long pantaloons; (2) a woollen shirt; (3) an outer mantle with a girdle round it. So these are specified [Gesenius], "their pantaloons, inner tunics (hosen, or stockings, are not commonly worn in the East), and outer mantles." Their being cast in so hurriedly, with all their garments on, enhanced the miracle in that not even the smell of fire passed on their clothes, though of delicate, inflammable material. <div eID="gen21689" type="x-p"/>
entries.49fcb2d32f8814987877cbfad82b0277a86dac4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12003"/><div sID="gen21690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12003"/><hi type="bold">22. flame ... slew those men--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.6.24">Da 6:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.16">Psa 7:16</reference>). <div eID="gen21690" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f8b56bcfbf1c948f2572238bba0f3244a28d48f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12004"/><div sID="gen21691" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12004"/><hi type="bold">23. fell down--</hi>not cast down; for those who brought the three youths to the furnace, perished by the flames themselves, and so could not cast them in. Here follows an addition in the Septuagint, Syrian, Arabic, and Vulgate versions. "The Prayer of Azarias," and "The Song of the Three Holy Children." It is not in the Chaldee. The hymn was sung throughout the whole Church in their liturgies, from the earliest times [Rufinus in Commentary on the Apostles Creed, and Athanasius]. The "astonishment" of Nebuchadnezzar in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.24">Da 3:24</reference> is made an argument for its genuineness, as if it explained the cause of his astonishment, namely, "they walked in the midst of the fire praising God, but the angel of the Lord came down into the oven" (vs. 1 and vs. 27 of the Apocryphal addition). But <reference osisRef="Dan.3.25">Da 3:25</reference> of English Version explains his astonishment, without need of any addition. <div eID="gen21691" type="x-p"/>
entries.bbcc26ae3900a823456d6912e15d8c51586f0d4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12005"/><div sID="gen21692" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12005"/><hi type="bold">24. True, O king--</hi>God extorted this confession from His enemies' own mouths. <div eID="gen21692" type="x-p"/>
entries.e50165f25b008bb141c4c45ad2f2c043e312e19e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12006"/><div sID="gen21693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12006"/><hi type="bold">25. four--</hi>whereas but three had been cast in.<div eID="gen21693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loose--</hi>whereas they had been cast in "bound." Nebuchadnezzar's question, in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.24">Da 3:24</reference>, is as if he can scarcely trust his own memory as to a fact so recent, now that he sees through an aperture in the furnace what seems to contradict it.<div eID="gen21694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walking in ... midst of ... fire--</hi>image of the godly unhurt, and at large (<reference osisRef="John.8.36">Joh 8:36</reference>), "in the midst of trouble" (<reference osisRef="Ps.138.7">Psa 138:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.23.3">Psa 23:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.23.4">4</reference>). They walked up and down in the fire, not leaving it, but waiting for God's time to bring them out, just as Jesus waited in the tomb as God's prisoner, till God should let Him out (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.26">Ac 2:26</reference>, 27). So Paul (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.8">2Co 12:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.9">9</reference>). So Noah waited in the ark, after the flood, till God brought him forth (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.12-Gen.8.18">Ge 8:12-18</reference>).<div eID="gen21695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">like the Son of God--</hi>Unconsciously, like Saul, Caiaphas (<reference osisRef="John.11.49-John.11.52">Joh 11:49-52</reference>), and Pilate, he is made to utter divine truths. "Son of God" in his mouth means only an "angel" from heaven, as <reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">Da 3:28</reference> proves. Compare <reference osisRef="Job.1.6">Job 1:6</reference>; 38:7; <reference osisRef="Ps.34.7">Psa 34:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.34.8">8</reference>; and the probably heathen centurion's exclamation (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.54">Mt 27:54</reference>). The Chaldeans believed in families of gods: Bel, the supreme god, accompanied by the goddess Mylitta, being the father of the gods; thus the expression he meant: one sprung from and sent by the gods. Really it was the "messenger of the covenant," who herein gave a prelude to His incarnation. <div eID="gen21696" type="x-p"/>
entries.4bc098d30cab17c35b86d8b1f287f587de5a3669: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12007"/><div sID="gen21697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12007"/><hi type="bold">26. the most high God--</hi>He acknowledges Jehovah to be supreme above other gods (not that he ceased to believe in these); so he returns to his original confession, "your God is a God of gods" (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.47">Da 2:47</reference>), from which he had swerved in the interim, perhaps intoxicated by his success in taking Jerusalem, whose God he therefore thought unable to defend it. <div eID="gen21697" type="x-p"/>
entries.782a0cc6d28e3d8ff201b90582bf10c41e266b24: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12008"/><div sID="gen21698" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12008"/><hi type="bold">27. nor ... an hair--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Luke.12.7">Lu 12:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.21.18">21:18</reference>).<div eID="gen21698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fire had no power--</hi>fulfilling <reference osisRef="Isa.43.2">Is 43:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.11.34">He 11:34</reference>. God alone is a "consuming fire" (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.29">He 12:29</reference>).<div eID="gen21699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21700" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor ... smell of fire--</hi>compare spiritually, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.22">1Th 5:22</reference>. <div eID="gen21700" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7f5e346dabb2239abf2792760f4e78b6f359240: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12009"/><div sID="gen21701" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12009"/>28. In giving some better traits in Nebuchadnezzar's character, Daniel agrees with <reference osisRef="Jer.39.11">Jr 39:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.42.12">42:12</reference>.<div eID="gen21701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">changed the king's word--</hi>have made the king's attempt to coerce into obedience vain. Have set aside his word (so "alter ... word," <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.11">Ezr 6:11</reference>) from regard to God. Nebuchadnezzar now admits that God's law should be obeyed, rather than his (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.29">Ac 5:29</reference>).<div eID="gen21702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">yielded ... bodies--</hi>namely, to the fire.<div eID="gen21703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21704" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not serve--</hi>by sacrificing.<div eID="gen21704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nor worship--</hi>by prostration of the body. Decision for God at last gains the respect even of the worldly (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.7">Pr 16:7</reference>). <div eID="gen21705" type="x-p"/>
entries.161614ec9824fb09b7460b326ca6ce0dcc4522a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12010"/><div sID="gen21706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12010"/>29. This decree promulgated throughout the vast empire of Nebuchadnezzar must have tended much to keep the Jews from idolatry in the captivity and thenceforth (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.10">Psa 76:10</reference>). <chapter eID="Dan.3"/>

entries.ed5e70a2b8cfaf2f307ab87796502a0d6a8b61d0: <div eID="gen32907" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen32908" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32909" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32909" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32908" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32910" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar, having erected an image, whose height (including probably a very high pedestal) was sixty cubits, and the breadth six, ordered a numerous assembly, which he had convened, to fall down and worship it; threatening, at the same time, that whosoever refused should be cast into a fiery furnace, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.1-Dan.3.7">Dan 3:1-7</reference>; a punishment not uncommon in that country, (see <reference osisRef="Jer.29.22">Jer 29:22</reference>.) Daniel's three companions, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, who were present, being observed to refrain from this idolatrous worship, were accused before the king; who, in great wrath, commanded them to comply with his orders on pain of death, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.8-Dan.3.15">Dan 3:8-15</reference>. But these holy men, with the greatest composure and serenity, expressed their firm resolution not to worship his gods or his images, whatever might be the consequence, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.16-Dan.3.18">Dan 3:16-18</reference>. Upon which the king, unaccustomed to have his will opposed, in the height of his wrath, ordered the furnace to be made seven times hotter than usual, and these men to be cast into it, bound by the most mighty of his army, who were killed by the flame in the execution of this service, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.19-Dan.3.23">Dan 3:19-23</reference>. On this occasion God literally performed his promise by Isaiah, (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.2">Isa 43:2</reference> ): "When thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burnt; neither shall the flame kindle upon thee;" for an angel of God, appearing in the furnace, protected these young men, and counteracted the natural violence of the fire; which, only consuming the cords with which they were bound, left them to walk at liberty, and in perfect safety, in the midst of the furnace. The king, astonished at this prodigy, called to them to come out of the furnace, and blessed God for sending an angel to deliver his servants; and commanded all his subjects, upon pain of death, not to speak irreverently of the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego, who were promoted to great power and honor, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.24-Dan.3.30">Dan 3:24-30</reference>. A striking example of the interposition of Providence in favor of true and inflexible piety. <div eID="gen32910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32911" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen32911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32912" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar the king made an image of gold - It is supposed that the history given here did not occur till the close, or near the end, of Nebuchadnezzar's reign. For it was after his insanity, as we see <reference osisRef="Dan.4.33-Dan.4.36">Dan 4:33-36</reference>, and this happened near the close of his reign. The authorized version, which is followed in the margin, fixes the date of this event seventeen years earlier, and ten years before the king's insanity. A few observations on this image may be necessary: - <div eID="gen32912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32913" type="x-p"/> 1. It is not likely that this image was in human form - the dimensions show the improbability of this; for what proportion is there between sixty cubits (ninety feet) in length, and six cubits (nine feet) in breadth? <div eID="gen32913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32914" type="x-p"/> 2. It is not likely that this image was all of gold; for this would have required more of this precious metal than the whole province of Babylon could produce; for as I suppose the sixty cubits apply to the perpendicular altitude, so I take it for granted that the six cubits intend the diameter. Now a column of gold of this height in diameter, upon the supposition that the pillar was circular, contains five thousand seven hundred and twenty-five and a half cubic feet; and as there are nineteen thousand avoirdupois ounces in a cubic foot, the weight of the whole pillar would be eight million two hundred and sixty-two thousand eight hundred and six pounds, ten ounces of gold. <div eID="gen32914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32915" type="x-p"/> 3. It might have been a pillar on which an image of the god Bel was erected. The image itself might be of gold, or more probably gilt, that is, covered with thin plates of gold, and on this account it might be called the golden image; and most probably the height of the image may be confounded with the height of the pillar. Or perhaps it was no more than a pillar, on the sides of which their gods and sacred emblems were engraven, surmounted with Bel on the top. <div eID="gen32915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32916" type="x-p"/> The plain of Dura - The situation of this place is not exactly known; there was a town or city called Dura, or Doura, in Mesopotamia, near the Tigris.
entries.6df34f7b326efabee08b739099e23d18fb233953: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen32916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32917" type="x-p"/> Sent to gather together the princes - It is not easy to show what these different offices were, as it is difficult to ascertain the meaning of the Chaldee words. Parkhurst analyzes them thus: - <div eID="gen32917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32918" type="x-p"/> The Princes - אחשדרפניא achashdarpenaiya, from אחש Achash, great or eminent, and דר dar, "to go about freely," and פנים panim, "the presence." Satraps or privy counsellors who had free access to the presence of the king. <div eID="gen32918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32919" type="x-p"/> The Governors - סגניא signaiya, lieutenants or viceroys, for סגן sagan, among the Hebrews, was the name of the high priest's deputy. <div eID="gen32919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32920" type="x-p"/> The Captains - פחותא pachavatha, from פח pach, to extend, because set over those provinces that had been annexed to the kingdom by conquest. Pashas - This word and office are still in use in Asiatic countries. By corruption we pronounce bashaw. <div eID="gen32920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32921" type="x-p"/> The Judges - אדרגזריא adargazeraiya, from אדר adar, noble or magnificent, and גזר gazar, to decree. The nobles, the assistants to the king in making laws, statutes, etc. The same probably in Babylon, as the House of Lords in England. <div eID="gen32921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32922" type="x-p"/> The Treasurers - גדבריא gedaberaiya, from גנז ganaz, (the ז zain being changed into ד daleth, according to the custom of the Chaldee), to treasure up, and בר bar, pure. Those who kept the current coin, or were over the mint; the treasurers of the exchequer in Babylon. <div eID="gen32922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32923" type="x-p"/> The Counsellors - דתבריא dethaberaiya, from דת dath, a statute, and בר bar, "to declare the meaning of the law;" for in all ages and countries there has been what is termed the glorious uncertainty of the law; and therefore there must be a class of men whose business it is to explain it. What a pity that law cannot be tendered to the people as other sciences are, in plain, unsophisticated, and intelligible terms, and by persons whose business it is to show what is just and right, and not pervert truth, righteousness, and judgment. <div eID="gen32923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32924" type="x-p"/> The Sheriffs - תפתיא tiphtaye, from תפת taphath, in Hebrew, שפת shaphath, "to set in order." Probably civil magistrates. <div eID="gen32924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32925" type="x-p"/> And all the rulers of the provinces - All other state or civil officers, not only to grace the solemnity, but to maintain order. My old Bible renders them: Satrapis, or wise men. Magistratis. Jugis. Duykis, Tyrauntis, or stronge men. Prefectis, and alle the Princes of Cuntreese.
entries.e9de9d91219a77d507a6b4b763f57d3691ba12ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen32925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32926" type="x-p"/> Then a herald cried aloud - כרוזא קרא בחיל caroza kara bechayil, "a crier called with might." A bedel cried mightili. - Old MS. Bible.
entries.8e588f04c8b1a13097d52544f27e96c68fee0158: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen32926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32927" type="x-p"/> The sound of the Cornet - There is not less difficulty in ascertaining the precise meaning of these musical instruments than there is in the offices in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.2">Dan 3:2</reference>. קרנא karna, here translated cornet, is the common blowing horn, which makes a deep and hollow sound, as well as one shrill and piercing. <div eID="gen32927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32928" type="x-p"/> Flute - משרוקיתא mashrokitha, from שרק sharak, to whistle, shriek. A wind instrument which made a strong and shrill noise, such as the hautbois or clarionet. <div eID="gen32928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32929" type="x-p"/> Harp - קיתרס kithros, cytharus; κιθαρα. Some kind of stringed instrument. It seems to be formed from the Greek word. <div eID="gen32929" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32930" type="x-p"/> Sackbut - סבכא sabbecha. The Greek has it σαμβυκη, from which our word sackbut, from סבך sabach, to interweave; probably on account of the number of chords, for it seems to have been a species of harp. <div eID="gen32930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32931" type="x-p"/> Psaltery - פסנתרין pesanterin; Greek, ψαλτηριον. A stringed instrument, struck with a plectrum; that called santeer in Egypt is probably the same. Dr. Russel says: "It is a large triangle, and has two bottoms two inches from each other, with about twenty catguts of different sizes." It was the ancient psalterium, and most probably the same as David's harp. <div eID="gen32931" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32932" type="x-p"/> Dulcimer - סומפניה sumponeyah; Greek, συμφωνεια. Probably a kind of tamboor, tambourine, or tomtom drum. It does not mean the same as the Greek symphonia, which signifies a concert or harmony of many instruments, for here one kind of instrument only is intended. <div eID="gen32932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32933" type="x-p"/> All kinds of music - כל זני זמרא col zeney zemara, the whole stock, or band, of music; the preceding being the chief, the most common, and the most sonorous. My old MS. Bible has, Trumpe, and Pipe, and Harpe: Sambuke, Santrie, and Synfonye, and al kynde of musykes.
entries.14be29fc1355779121cdc97747acdaade44ad32d: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen32933" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32934" type="x-p"/> Shall the same hour - This is the first place in the Old Testament where we find the division of time into hours. The Greeks say that Anaximander was the inventor. He had it probably from the Chaldeans, among whom this division was in use long before Anaximander was born. <div eID="gen32934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32935" type="x-p"/> Be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace - This was an ancient mode of punishment among the Chaldeans, if we may credit the tradition that Abram was cast into such a fire by this idolatrous people because he would not worship their idols.
entries.e5a81966f9ef4e915f81eef18749f05e69014007: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen32935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32936" type="x-p"/> Accused the Jews - That is, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abed-nego. The other Jews were left unnoticed; and probably at this time Daniel was too high to be touched; but we may rest assured that he was not found among these idolaters, see <reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">Dan 3:12</reference>.
entries.bd104e9ac20b6bd2fdad4fed3f8dbcd5fbcff718: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen32936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32937" type="x-p"/> We are not careful - We have no need to put thee to any farther trouble; we have made up our minds on this subject, and have our answer ready: Be it known unto thee, We Will Not Serve Thy Gods. This was as honest as it was decisive.
entries.87423abd26e3ecafa0c229a216f0a26562f7d703: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen32937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32938" type="x-p"/> If it be so - Thou mayest cast us into the furnace; the terror of it has no effect on our minds to induce us to alter the resolution we have taken, nor shall the fire change our purpose. We serve a God who is able to deliver us. Should he not, we are equally determined; but we are satisfied that in some way or other he will deliver us out of thy hand. Thy power cannot affect us in the kingdom of our God to which we shall ascend from thy furnace, should he permit the fire to kindle upon us. "Render to Caesar the things which are Caesar's," is a maxim of Jesus Christ; but when Caesar arrogates to himself the things that are the Lord's, then, and in such cases, his authority is to be resisted. God does not desire Caesar's things; Caesar's must not have the things of God.
entries.4d183080026cc8a5011ede9ed5fdc59540210bdc: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen32938" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32939" type="x-p"/> Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury - How strange is this, after having had so many proofs of the supremacy of Jehovah! He had seen how God poured contempt upon his authority in the case of the three Hebrews, and yet he will try his strength once more! How infatuated is man! <div eID="gen32939" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32940" type="x-p"/> Seven times more - As hot as it could be made. Seven expresses the great intensity of the heat.
entries.bc35b96e54c0b11558a95ec81dfb6f20f5dfdd96: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen32940" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32941" type="x-p"/> The most mighty men - The generals, or chief officers of his army; not strong men, there was no need of such.
entries.4ff24cabe88b12f211f8efa914ec44932c9d2518: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen32941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32942" type="x-p"/> Their hats - This word, hat, is found only in this place in the Old Testament. The word סרבל sarbal properly means an outer garment. Herodotus, who lived about one hundred years after Daniel, says, "the dress of the Babylonians consisted of a tunic of linen reaching down to the feet; over this a tunic of woollen; and over all a white short cloak or mantle, χλανιδιον; and on their heads they wore turbans, μιτρησι." Following this, Mr. Parkhurst translates the verse thus: "Then these three men were bound [בסרבליהון besarbaleyhon] in their Cloaks, [פמישיהון patesheyhon] their Turbans, [וכרבלתהון vecharbelathehon] and in their Upper (woollen) Tunics, [ולבושיהון ulebushehon] and their Under (linen) Tunics." And as, according to this interpretation, their סרבלי sarbaley were their outermost garments, we see the propriety with which it is observed at <reference osisRef="Dan.3.27">Dan 3:27</reference> that these were not changed by the fire.
entries.49dfaeae90779c57d7ebb25aa8a1d7a0892b6793: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen32942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32943" type="x-p"/> And these three men - fell down bound - There is a most evident want of connection between this and the following verse; and it is between these verses that the apocryphal Song of the Three Children, as it is called, has been inserted by St. Jerome and others; but with this note: Quae sequuntur in Hebraeis voluminibus non reperi; "What follows I have not found in the Hebrew books." And then begins, "They walked in the midst of the flame, praising God, and blessing the Lord." The Septuagint and Arabic read the twenty-fourth verse thus: "Then Nebuchadnezzar heard them singing praise, and was astonished." To connect the two verses Houbigant adds two verses found in the Vulgate, which are the forty-ninth and the twenty-third: "But an angel of the Lord went down with Azariah and his companions into the furnace, and drove out the flame of fire from the furnace; and they walked in the midst of the furnace." This verse (the forty-ninth) has been added to show the reason of Nebuchadnezzar's astonishment, and also to account for the appearance of a fourth person in the furnace, as in verse 25.
entries.194e7a8b79c4468d065a217c137b236a16c7d324: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen32943" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32944" type="x-p"/> Is like the Son of God - A most improper translation. What notion could this idolatrous king have of the Lord Jesus Christ? for so the place is understood by thousands. בר אלהין bar elahin signifies a son of the gods, that is, a Divine person or angel; and so the king calls him in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">Dan 3:28</reference> : "God hath sent his Angel, and delivered his servants." And though even from this some still contend that it was the Angel of the covenant, yet the Babylonish king knew just as much of the one as he did of the other. No other ministration was necessary; a single angel from heaven was quite sufficient to answer this purpose, as that which stopped the mouths of the lions when Daniel was cast into their den.
entries.94bec42036f82dc3dde0cdcd0db8cd4567015bfb: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen32944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32945" type="x-p"/> Upon whose bodies the fire had no power - The heathens boasted that their priests could walk on burning coals unhurt; and Virgil mentions this of the priests of Apollo of Soracte: - <div eID="gen32945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32946" type="x-p"/> Summe Deum, sancti custos Soractis Apollo! <div eID="gen32946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32947" type="x-p"/> Quem primi colimus, cui pineus ardor acervo <div eID="gen32947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32948" type="x-p"/> Pascitur; et medium, freti pietate, per ignem <div eID="gen32948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32949" type="x-p"/> Cultores multa premimus vestigia pruna. <div eID="gen32949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32950" type="x-p"/> Virg. Aen. 11:785. <div eID="gen32950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32951" type="x-p"/> O Phoebus, guardian of Soracte's woods <div eID="gen32951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32952" type="x-p"/> And shady hills; a god above the gods; <div eID="gen32952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32953" type="x-p"/> To whom our natives pay the rites divine, <div eID="gen32953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32954" type="x-p"/> And burn whole crackling groves of hallowed pine; <div eID="gen32954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32955" type="x-p"/> Walk through the fire in honor of thy name, <div eID="gen32955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32956" type="x-p"/> Unhurt, unsinged, and sacred from the flame. <div eID="gen32956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32957" type="x-p"/> Pitts. <div eID="gen32957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32958" type="x-p"/> But Varro tells us that they anointed the soles of their feet with a species of unguent that preserved them from being burnt. Very lately a female showed many feats of this kind, putting red hot iron upon her arms, breasts, etc., and passing it over her hair without the slightest inconvenience; but in the case of the three Hebrews all was supernatural, and the king and his officers well knew it.
entries.a020e08e68a37d41c65204615f5f018501e6efd5: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen32958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32959" type="x-p"/> Blessed be the God of Shadrach, etc. - Here is a noble testimony from a heathen. And what produced it? The intrepidly pious conduct of these three noble Jews. Had they been time-servers, the name of the true God had not been known in Babylon. What honor does the Lord put on them that are steadfast in the faith!
entries.f660d28fa3f80300a125e0f1e9f6fa3c2e9d9e17: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen32959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32960" type="x-p"/> Speak any thing amiss - Though by the decree the king does not oblige the people to worship the true God, yet he obliges them to treat him with reverence.
entries.b6d9dd99d4173a0b2a802566ee0125d15c44be28: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen32960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32961" type="x-p"/> Then the king promoted, etc. - He restored them to the offices which they held before the charge of disobedience and treason was brought against them. <div eID="gen32961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32962" type="x-p"/> At the end of this verse the Septuagint add, "And he advanced them to be governors over all the Jews that were in his kingdom." This may be the meaning of the latter verse. They were more likely to be set over the Jews than over the Chaldeans.  <chapter eID="Dan.3"/> <div eID="gen32962" type="x-p"/>

entries.b6b9ec500932bc605441c1f596cc6dc99392eea4: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.1">Dan 3:1</reference> <div eID="gen15546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15547" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar commanded a golden image to be erected, of threescore cubits in height and six cubits in breadth. צלם is properly <hi type="italic">an image in human likeness</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.2.31">Dan 2:31</reference>), and excludes the idea of a mere pillar or an obelisk, for which מצּבה would have been the appropriate word. Yet from the use of the word צלם it is not by any means to be concluded that the image was in all respects perfectly in human form. As to the upper part - the head, countenance, arms, breast - it may have been in the form of a man, and the lower part may have been formed like a pillar. This would be altogether in accordance with the Babylonian art, which delighted in grotesque, gigantic forms; cf. Hgstb. <hi type="italic">Beitr</hi>. i. p. 96f. The measure, in height threescore cubits, in breadth six cubits, is easily explained, since in the human figure the length is to be breadth in the proportion of about six to one. In the height of threescore cubits the pedestal of the image may be regarded as included, so that the whole image according to its principal component part (<hi type="italic">a potiori</hi>) was designated as צלם; although the passage Jdg 18:30-31, adduced by Kran., where mention is made of the image alone which was erected by Micah, without any notice being taken of the pedestal belonging to it (cf. Jdg 18:17 and Jdg 18:18), furnishes no properly authentic proof that פּסל in Jdg 18:30 and Jdg 18:31 denotes the image with the pedestal. The proportion between the height and the breadth justifies, then, in no respect the rejection of the historical character of the narrative. Still less does the mass of gold necessary for the construction of so colossal an image, since, as has been already mentioned, according to the Hebrew modes of speech, we are not required to conceive of the figure as having been made of solid gold, and since, in the great riches of the ancient world, Nebuchadnezzar in his successful campaigns might certainly accumulate an astonishing amount of this precious metal. The statements of Herodotus and Diodorus regarding the Babylonian idol-images,<note placement="foot">According to Herod. i. 183, for the great golden image of Belus, which was twelve cubits high, and the great golden table standing before it, the golden steps and the golden chair, only 800 talents of gold were used; and according to Diod. Sic. ii. 9, the golden statue, forty feet high, placed in the temple of Belus consisted of 1000 talents of gold, which would have been not far from sufficient if these objects had been formed of solid gold. Diod. also expressly says regarding the statue, that it was made with the hammer, and therefore was not solid. Cf. Hgstb. <hi type="italic">Beitr</hi>. i. p. 98, and Kran. <hi type="italic">in loco</hi>.</note> as well as the description in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.19">Isa 40:19</reference> of the construction of idol-images, lead us to think of the image as merely overlaid with plates of gold. <div eID="gen15547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15548" type="x-p"/> The king commanded this image to be set up in the plain of <hi type="italic">Dura</hi> in the province of Babylon. The ancients make mention of two places of the name of <hi type="italic">Dura</hi>, the one at the mouth of the Chaboras where it empties itself into the Euphrates, not far from Carchemish (Polyb. v. 48; Ammian. Marc. xxiii. 5, 8, xxiv. 1, 5), the other beyond the Tigris, not far from Apollonia (Polyb. v. 52; Amm. Marc. xxv. 6, 9). Of these the latter has most probability in its favour, since the former certainly did not belong to the province of Babylon, which according to Xenophon extended 36 miles south of Tiphsach (cf. Nieb. <hi type="italic">Gesch. Assurs</hi>, S. 421). The latter, situated in the district of Sittakene, could certainly be reckoned as belonging to the province of Babylon, since according to Strabo, Sittakene, at least in the Old Parthian time, belonged to Babylon (Nieb. p. 420). But even this place lay quite too far from the capital of the kingdom to be the place intended. We must, without doubt, much rather seek for this plain in the neighbourhood of Babylon, where, according to the statement of Jul. Oppert (<hi type="italic">Expéd. Scientif. en Mésopotamie</hi>, i. p. 238ff.), there are at present to be found in the S.S.E. of the ruins representing the former capital a row of mounds which bear the name of Dura, at the end of which, along with two larger mounds, there is a smaller one which is named <hi type="italic">el Mokattat</hi> (=<hi type="italic">la colline alignée</hi>), which forms a square six metres high, with a basis of fourteen metres, wholly built <hi type="italic">en briques crues</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">lbn</hi>), which shows so surprising a resemblance to a colossal statue with its pedestal, that Oppert believes that this little mound is the remains of the golden statue erected by Nebuchadnezzar.<note placement="foot">“On seeing this mound,” Oppert remarks (<hi type="italic">l. c.</hi> p. 239), “one is immediately struck with the resemblance which it presents to the pedestal of a colossal statue, as, for example, that of Bavaria near Münich, and everything leads to the belief that the statue mentioned in the book of Daniel (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.1">Dan 3:1</reference>) was set up in this place. The fact of the erection by Nebuchadnezzar of a colossal statue has nothing which can cause astonishment, however recent may have been the Aramean form of the account of Scripture.” Oppert, moreover, finds no difficulty in the size of the statue, but says regarding it: “There is nothing incredible in the existence of a statue sixty cubits high and six cubits broad; moreover the name of the plain of Dura, in the province (מדינה) of Babylon, agrees also with the actual conformation of the ruin.”</note> <div eID="gen15548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15549" type="x-p"/> There is a difference of opinion as to the signification of this image. According to the common view (cf. e.g., Hgstb. <hi type="italic">Beitr</hi>. i. p. 97), Nebuchadnezzar wished to erect a statue as an expression of his thanks to his god Bel for his great victories, and on that account also to consecrate it with religious ceremonies. On the other hand, Hofm. (<hi type="italic">Weiss. u. Erf.</hi> i. p. 277) remarks, that the statue was not the image of a god, because a distinction is made between falling down to it and the service to his god which Nebuchadnezzar required (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">Dan 3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.14">Dan 3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.18">Dan 3:18</reference>) from his officers of state. This distinction, however, is not well supported; for in these verses praying to the gods of Nebuchadnezzar is placed on an equality with falling down before the image. But on the other hand, the statue is not designated as the image of a god, or the image of Belus; therefore we agree with Klief. in his opinion, that the statue was a symbol of the world-power established by Nebuchadnezzar, so that falling down before it was a manifestation of reverence not only to the world-power, but also to its gods; and that therefore the Israelites could not fall down before the image, because in doing so they would have rendered homage at the same time also to the god or gods of Nebuchadnezzar, in the image of the world-power. But the idea of representing the world-power founded by him as a צלם  was probably suggested to Nebuchadnezzar by the tselem seen (Daniel 2) by him in a dream, whose head of gold his world-kingdom was described to him as being. We may not, however, with Klief., seek any sanction for the idea that the <hi type="italic">significance</hi> off the image is in its size, 6, 10, and six multiplied by ten cubits, because the symbolical significance of the number 6 as the signature of human activity, to which the divine completion (7) is wanting, is not a Babylonian idea. Still less can we, with Zündel (p. 13), explain the absence of Daniel on this occasion as arising from the political import of the statue, because the supposition of Daniel’s not having been called to be present is a mere conjecture, and a very improbable conjecture; and the supposition that Daniel, as being chief of the Magi, would not be numbered among the secular officers of state, is decidedly erroneous.
entries.06be6fd42cd5666baa8bd58705e1a507169bda5f: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.2-Dan.3.7">Dan 3:2-7</reference> <div eID="gen15549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15550" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar commanded all the chief officers of the kingdom to be present at the solemn dedication of the image. שׁלח, <hi type="italic">he sent</hi>, viz., מלאכים or רצים <hi type="italic">messengers</hi>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.11.7">1Sa 11:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.6">2Ch 30:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.10">2Ch 30:10</reference>; Est 3:15. Of the great officers of state, seven classes are named: - 1. אחשׁדּרפּניּא, i.e., <hi type="italic">administrators</hi> of the <hi type="italic">Khshatra</hi>, in Old Pers. <hi type="italic">dominion</hi>, <hi type="italic">province</hi>, and <hi type="italic">pâvan</hi> in Zend., <hi type="italic">guardians</hi>, <hi type="italic">watchers</hi>, in Greek Σατράπης, the chief representatives of the king in the provinces. 2. סגניּא, Hebr. סגנים, from the Old Pers. (although not proved) <hi type="italic">çakana</hi>, <hi type="italic">to command</hi> (see under <reference osisRef="Dan.2.48">Dan 2:48</reference>), <hi type="italic">commanders</hi>, probably <hi type="italic">the military chiefs of the provinces</hi>. 3. פּחותא, Hebr. פּחה, פחות, also an Old Pers. word, whose etymon and meaning have not yet been established (see under Hag 1:1), denotes <hi type="italic">the presidents of the civil government, the guardians of the country</hi>; cf. Hag 1:1, Hag 1:14; <reference osisRef="Neh.5.14">Neh 5:14</reference>, Neh 5:18. 4. אדרגּזריּא, <hi type="italic">chief judges</hi>, from the Sem. גזר, to distinguish, and אדר, dignity (cf. אדרמּלך), properly, <hi type="italic">chief arbitrators, counsellors of the government</hi>. 5. גּדבריּא, a word of Aryan origin, from גּדבר, identical with גּזבּר, <hi type="italic">masters of the treasury, superintendents of the public treasury</hi>. 6. דּתבריּא, the Old Pers. <hi type="italic">dâta - bara</hi>, <hi type="italic">guardians of the law, lawyers</hi> (cf. דּת, law). 7. תּפתּיּא, Semitic, from Arab. <hi type="italic">fty</hi> IV <hi type="italic">to give a just sentence</hi>, thus <hi type="italic">judges</hi> in the narrower sense of the word. Finally, all שׁלטני, <hi type="italic">rulers</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">governors of provinces</hi>, prefects, who were subordinate to the chief governor, cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.2.48">Dan 2:48</reference>-49. <div eID="gen15550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15551" type="x-p"/> All these officers were summoned “to come (מתא from אתא, with the rejection of the initial )א to the dedication of the image.” The objection of v. Leng. and Hitz., that this call would “put a stop to the government of the country,” only shows their ignorance of the departments of the state-government, and by no means makes the narrative doubtful. The affairs of the state did not lie so exclusively in the hands of the presidents of the different branches of the government, as that their temporary absence should cause a suspension of all the affairs of government. חנכּה is used of the dedication of a house (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.5">Deu 20:5</reference>) as well as of the temple (1Ki 8:63; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.5">2Ch 7:5</reference>; Ezr 6:16), and here undoubtedly denotes an act connected with religious usages, by means of which the image, when the great officers of the kingdom fell down before it, was solemnly consecrated as the symbol of the world-power and (in the heathen sense) of its divine glory. This act is described (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.3-Dan.3.7">Dan 3:3-7</reference>) in so far as the object contemplated rendered it necessary. <div eID="gen15551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15552" type="x-p"/> When all the great officers of state were assembled, a herald proclaimed that as soon as the sound of the music was heard, all who were present should, on pain of death by being cast into the fire, fall down before the image and offer homage to it; which they all did as soon as the signal was given. The form קאמין, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.3">Dan 3:3</reference>, corresponds to the sing. קאם (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.31">Dan 2:31</reference>) as it is written in Syr., but is read קימין. The Masoretes substitute for it in the Talm. The common form קימין; cf. Fürst, <hi type="italic">Lehrgb. der aram. Idiom.</hi> p. 161, and Luzzatto, <hi type="italic">Elem. Gram.</hi> p. 33. The expression לקבל, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.3">Dan 3:3</reference>, and Ezr 4:16, is founded on קבל, the semi-vowel of the preceding sound being absorbed, as in the Syr. <hi type="italic">lû-kebel</hi>. On כּרוזא, <hi type="italic">herald</hi>, and on the form לכון, see under Dan 2:5. אמרין, <hi type="italic">they say</hi>, for “it is said to you.” The expression of the passive by means of a plural form of the active used impersonally, either participially or by 3rd pers. perf. plur., is found in Hebr., but is quite common in Chald.; cf. Ewald, <hi type="italic">Lehr. d. hebr. Spr.</hi> §128, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, and Winer, <hi type="italic">Chald. Gram.</hi> §49, 3. The proclamation of the herald refers not only to the officers who were summoned to the festival, but to all who were present, since besides the officers there was certainly present a great crowd of people from all parts of the kingdom, as M. Geier has rightly remarked, so that the assembly consisted of persons of various races and languages. אמּיּא denotes <hi type="italic">tribes of people</hi>, as the Hebr. אמּה, אמּות <reference osisRef="Gen.25.16">Gen 25:16</reference>, denotes the several tribes of Ishmael, and Num 25:15 the separate tribes of the Midianites, and is thus not so extensive in its import as עמּין, <hi type="italic">peoples</hi>. לשּׁניּא, corresponding to הלּשׁות, <reference osisRef="Isa.66.18">Isa 66:18</reference>, designates (<hi type="italic">vide</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.10.5">Gen 10:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.20">Gen 10:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.10.31">Gen 10:31</reference>) <hi type="italic">communities of men of the same language</hi>, and is not a tautology, since the distinctions of nation and of language are in the course of history frequently found. The placing together of the three words denotes all nations, however they may have widely branched off into tribes with different languages, and expresses the sense that no one in the whole kingdom should be exempted from the command. It is a mode of expression (cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.3.7">Dan 3:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.29">Dan 3:29</reference>, 31[4:1], and Dan 6:26[25]) specially characterizing the pathetic style of the herald and the official language of the world-kingdom, which Daniel also (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.19">Dan 5:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Dan 7:14</reference>) makes use of, and which from the latter passage is transferred to the Apocalypse, and by the union of these passages in Daniel with <reference osisRef="Isa.66.18">Isa 66:18</reference> is increased to ἔθνη (גּוים in Isa.), φυλλαι,́ λαοὶ καὶ γλῶσσαι (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.9">Rev 5:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.7.9">Rev 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.7">Rev 13:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6">Rev 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.17.15">Rev 17:15</reference>). <div eID="gen15552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15553" type="x-p"/> In the same passage זמנא בּהּ, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.7">Dan 3:7</reference> (cf. also <reference osisRef="Dan.3.8">Dan 3:8</reference>), is interchanged with בּעדּנא, <hi type="italic">at the time</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.5">Dan 3:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">Dan 3:15</reference>); but it is to be distinguished from בּהּ־שׁעתּא, <hi type="italic">at the same moment</hi>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.6">Dan 3:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">Dan 3:15</reference>; for שׁעא or שׁעה has in the Bib. Chald. only the meaning <hi type="italic">instant</hi>, <hi type="italic">moment</hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.4.16">Dan 4:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.30">Dan 4:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.5.5">Dan 5:5</reference>, and acquires the signification <hi type="italic">short time, hour</hi>, first in the Targ. and Rabbin. In the enumeration also of the six names of the musical instruments with the addition: <hi type="italic">and all kinds of music</hi>, the pompous language of the world-ruler and of the herald of his power is well expressed. Regarding the Greek names of three of these instruments see p. 507. The great delight of the Babylonians in music and stringed instruments appears from <reference osisRef="Isa.14.11">Isa 14:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.137.3">Psa 137:3</reference>, and is confirmed by the testimony of Herod. i. 191, and Curtius, Dan 3:3. קרנא, <hi type="italic">horn</hi>, is the far-sounding <hi type="italic">tuba</hi> of the ancients, the קרן or שׁופר of the Hebr.; see under Jos 6:5. משׁרוקיתא, from שׁרק, <hi type="italic">to hiss, to whistle</hi>, is the <hi type="italic">reed-flute</hi>, translated by the lxx and Theodot. σύριγξ, the <hi type="italic">shepherd's</hi> or <hi type="italic">Pan’s pipes</hi>, which consisted of several reeds of different thicknesses and of different lengths bound together, and, according to a Greek tradition (Pollux, iv. 9, 15), was invented by two Medes. קיתתס (according to the <hi type="italic">Kethiv</hi>; but the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> and the Targ. and Rabbin. give the form קתרס) is the Greek κιθάρα or κίθαρις, <hi type="italic">harp</hi>, for the Greek ending ις becomes ος in the Aramaic, as in many similar cases; cf. Ges.<hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 1215. סבּכא, corresponding to the Greek σαμβύκη, but a Syrian invention, is, according to Athen. iv. p. 175, <hi type="italic">a four-stringed instrument</hi>, having a sharp, clear tone; cf. Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes.</hi> p. 935. פּסנמּרין (in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.7">Dan 3:7</reference> written with a  טinstead of  תand in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.10">Dan 3:10</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">Dan 3:15</reference> pointed with a Tsere under the )ת is the Greek ψαλτήριον, of which the Greek ending ιον becomes abbreviated in the Aram. into ין  (cf. Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 1116). The word has no etymology in the Semitic. It was an instrument like a harp, which according to Augustin (on <reference osisRef="Ps.33.2">Psa 33:2</reference> [32:2] and <reference osisRef="Ps.43.4">Psa 43:4</reference> [42:4) was distinguished from the <hi type="italic">cithara</hi> in this particular, that while the strings of the <hi type="italic">cithara</hi> passed over the sounding-board, those of the <hi type="italic">psalterium</hi> (or <hi type="italic">organon</hi>) were placed under it. Such harps are found on Egyptian (see Rosellini) and also on Assyrian monuments (cf. Layard, <hi type="italic">Ninev</hi>. and <hi type="italic">Bab</hi>., Table xiii. 4). סוּמפּניה, in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.10">Dan 3:10</reference> סיפניה, is not derived from ספן, <hi type="italic">contignare</hi>, but is the Aramaic form of συμφωνία, <hi type="italic">bag-pipes</hi>, which is called in Italy at the present day <hi type="italic">sampogna</hi>, and derives its Greek name from the accord of two pipes placed in the bag; cf. Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes.</hi> p. 941. זמרא signifies, not “song,” but <hi type="italic">musical playing</hi>, from reemaz, <hi type="italic">to play the strings</hi>, ψάλλειν; and because the music of the instrument was accompanied with song, it means also <hi type="italic">the song accompanying the music</hi>. The explanation of זמרא by singing stands here in opposition to the זני כּל, since all sorts of songs could only be sung after one another, but the herald speaks of the simultaneous rise of the sound. The limiting of the word also to the playing on a stringed instrument does not fit the context, inasmuch as wind instruments are also named. Plainly in the words זמרא זני כּל all the other instruments not particularly named are comprehended, so that זמרא is to be understood generally of <hi type="italic">playing on musical instruments</hi>. בּהּ־שׁעתּא, <hi type="italic">in the same instant</hi>. The frequent pleonastic use in the later Aramaic of the union of the preposition with a suffix anticipating the following noun, whereby the preposition is frequently repeated before the noun, as e.g., בּדּניּאל בּהּ, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.12">Dan 5:12</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Dan.5.30">Dan 5:30</reference>, has in the Bibl. Chald. generally a certain emphasis, for the pronominal suffix is manifestly used demonstratively, in the sense <hi type="italic">even</hi> this, <hi type="italic">even</hi> that. <div eID="gen15553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15554" type="x-p"/> Homage was commanded to be shown to the image under the pain of death to those who refused. Since “the dominion of Nebuchadnezzar was founded not by right, but by the might of conquest” (Klief.), and the homage which he commanded to be shown to the image was regarded not only as a proof of subjection under the power of the king, but comprehended in it also the recognition of his gods as the gods of the kingdom, instances of refusal were to be expected. In the demand of the king there was certainly a kind of religious oppression, but by no means, as Bleek, v. Leng., and other critics maintain, a religious persecution, as among heathen rulers Antiochus Epiphanes practised it. For so tolerant was heathenism, that it recognised the gods of the different nations; but all heathen kings required that the nations subdued by them should also recognise the gods of their kingdom, which they held to be more powerful than were the gods of the vanquished nations. A refusal to yield homage to the gods of the kingdom they regarded as an act of hostility against the kingdom and its monarch, while every one might at the same time honour his own national god. This acknowledgement, that the gods of the kingdom were the more powerful, every heathen could grant; and thus Nebuchadnezzar demanded nothing in a religious point of view which every one of his subjects could not yield. To him, therefore, the refusal of the Jews could not but appear as opposition to the greatness of his kingdom. But the Jews, or Israelites, could not do homage to the gods of Nebuchadnezzar without rejecting their faith that Jehovah alone was God, and that besides Him there were no gods. Therefore Nebuchadnezzar practised towards them, without, from his polytheistic standpoint, designing it, an intolerable religious coercion, which, whoever, is fundamentally different from the persecution of Judaism by Antiochus Epiphanes, who forbade the Jews on pain of death to serve their God, and endeavoured utterly to destroy the Jewish religion. - Regarding the structure of the fiery furnace, see under Dan 3:22.
entries.af941038ec16bd84f0b1e42d4cb6ba5f70a4cbf3: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.8-Dan.3.12">Dan 3:8-12</reference> <div eID="gen15554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15555" type="x-p"/> The Chaldeans immediately denounced Daniel’s three friends as transgressors of the king’s command. דּנה כּל־קבל, <hi type="italic">therefore</hi>, viz., because the friends of Daniel who were placed over the province of Babylon had not, by falling down before the golden image, done it homage. That they did not do so is not expressly said, but is expressed in what follows. כּשׂדּאין גּברין are not Chaldeans as astrologers of magi (כּשׂדּים), but members of the Chaldean nation, in contrast to יהוּדיא, the Jews. קרבוּ, <hi type="italic">they came near to the king</hi>. דּי קרצי אכל, literally, <hi type="italic">to eat the flesh of any one</hi>, is in Aramaic the common expression for <hi type="italic">to calumniate, to denounce</hi>. That which was odious in their report was, that they used this instance of disobedience to the king’s command on the part of the Jewish officers as an occasion of removing them from their offices, - that their denunciation of them arose from their envying the Jews their position of influence, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.6.5">Dan 6:5</reference> (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.4">4</reference>)f. Therefore they give prominence to the fact that the king had raised these Jews to places of rule in the province of Babylon. <div eID="gen15555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15556" type="x-p"/> With this form of address in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.9">Dan 3:9</reference>, cf. Dan 2:4. טעם שׂים signifies in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">Dan 3:12</reference> <hi type="italic">rationem reddere</hi>, to attend to, to have regard for. In <reference osisRef="Dan.3.10">Dan 3:10</reference>, as frequently, the expression signifies, on the contrary, <hi type="italic">to give an opinion, a judgment</hi>, i.e., <hi type="italic">to publish a command</hi>. The <hi type="italic">Keth</hi>. לאלהיך (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.12">Dan 3:12</reference>), for which the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> prefers the sing. form לאלהך, in sound the same as the contracted plur., is to be maintained as correct; for the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> here, as in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.18">Dan 3:18</reference>, supporting itself on לאלהי, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.14">Dan 3:14</reference>, rests on the idea that by the honouring of his god only the doing of homage to the image is meant, while the not doing homage to the image only gives proof of this, that they altogether refused to honour the gods of Nebuchadnezzar. This is placed in the foreground by the accusers, so as to arouse the indignation of the king. “These Chaldeans,” Hitz. remarks quite justly, “knew the three Jews, who were so placed as to be well known, and at the same time envied, before this. They had long known that they did not worship idols; but on this occasion, when their religion made it necessary for the Jews to disobey the king’s command, they make use of their knowledge.”
entries.f8695621903f85ebad699ebfb0a555084cc759ae: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.13">Dan 3:13</reference> <div eID="gen15556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15557" type="x-p"/> That they succeeded in their object, Nebuchadnezzar shows in the command given in anger and fury to bring the rebels before him. היתיוּ, notwithstanding its likeness to the Hebr. Hiphil form התיוּ, <reference osisRef="Isa.21.14">Isa 21:14</reference>, is not the Hebraizing Aphel, but, as היתית, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.18">Dan 6:18</reference>, shows, is a Hebraizing passive from of the Aphel, since the active form is היתיו, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.3">Dan 5:3</reference>, and is a passive formation peculiar to the Bib. Chald, for which in the Targg. Ittaphal is used.<hi type="italic">The trial of the accused</hi>.
entries.ed2068658c54fb063602a9fb42d9706f35ea6f60: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.14">Dan 3:14</reference> <div eID="gen15557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15558" type="x-p"/> The question הצדא the old translators incorrectly explain by Is it true? In the justice of the accusation Nebuchadnezzar had no doubt whatever, and צדא has not this meaning. Also the meaning, <hi type="italic">scorn</hi>, which אּצדי in Aram. has, and L. de Dieu, Häv., and Kran. make use of, does not appear to be quite consistent, since Nebuchadnezzar, if he had seen in the refusal to do homage to the image a despising of his gods, then certainly he would not have publicly repeated his command, and afforded to the accused the possibility of escaping the threatened punishment, as he did (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">Dan 3:15</reference>). We therefore agree with Hitz. and Klief., who interpret it, after the Hebr. צדיּה, Num 35:20., of <hi type="italic">malicious resolution</hi>, not merely intention, according to Gesen., Winer, and others. For all the three could not unintentionally or accidentally have made themselves guilty of transgression. The form הצדא we regard as a noun form with  הinterrog. prefixed in adverbial cases, and not an Aphel formation: <hi type="italic">Scorning, Shadrach, etc., do ye not serve?</hi> (Kran.) The affirmative explanation of the verse, according to which the king would suppose the motive of the transgression as decided, does not agree with the alternative which (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">Dan 3:15</reference>) he places before the accused. But if הצדא is regarded as a question, there is no need for our supplying the conjunction דּי before the following verb, but we may unite the חצדא in one sentence with the following verb: “<hi type="italic">are ye of design ... not obeying?</hi>” Nebuchadnezzar speaks of his god in contrast to the God of the Jews.
entries.357e5cda57e8da1162ba770add2ff4b2f62d32ef: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">Dan 3:15</reference> עתידין taken with the following clause, תּפּלוּן ... דּי, is not a circumlocution for the future (according to Winer, <hi type="italic">Chald. Gram.</hi> §45, 2). This does not follow from the use of the simple future in contrast, but it retains its peculiar meaning <hi type="italic">ready</hi>. The conclusion to the first clause is omitted, because it is self-evident from the conclusion of the second, opposed passage: <hi type="italic">then ye will not be cast into the fiery furnace</hi>. Similar omissions are found in <reference osisRef="Exod.32.32">Exo 32:32</reference>; Luk 13:9. For the purpose of giving strength to his threatening, Nebuchadnezzar adds that no god would deliver them out of his hand. In this Hitz. is not justified in supposing there is included a blaspheming of Jehovah like that of Sennacherib, Isa 37:10. The case is different. Sennacherib raised his gods above Jehovah, the God of the Jews; Nebuchadnezzar only declares that deliverance out of the fiery furnace is a work which no god can accomplish, and in this he only indirectly likens the God of the Jews to the gods of the heathen.
entries.2f0145debe82db04f30723661653a32e22ccc2ba: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.16">Dan 3:16</reference> <div eID="gen15558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15559" type="x-p"/> In the answer of the accused, נבוּכדנצּר is not, contrary to the accent, to be placed in apposition to למלכּא; for, as Kran. has rightly remarked, an intentional omission of מלכּא in addressing Nebuchadnezzar is, after <reference osisRef="Dan.3.18">Dan 3:18</reference>, where מלכּא occurs in the address, as little likely as that the Athnach is placed under למלכּא only on account of the apposition going before, to separate from it the <hi type="italic">nomen propr.</hi>; and an error in the placing of the <hi type="italic">distinctivus</hi>, judging from the existing accuracy, is untenable. “The direct address of the king by his name plainly corresponds to the king’s address to the three officers in the preceding words, Dan 3:14.” We are not to conclude from it, as Hitz. supposes, “that they address him as a plebeian,” but much rather, as in the corresponding address, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.14">Dan 3:14</reference>, are to see in it an evidence of the deep impression sought to be produced in the person concerned. פּתגּם is the accus., and is not to be connected with דּנה על: <hi type="italic">as to this command</hi> (Häv.). If the demonstrative were present only before the noun, then the noun must stand in the <hi type="italic">status absol.</hi> as <reference osisRef="Dan.4.15">Dan 4:15</reference> (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.18">18</reference>). פּתגּם, from the Zend. <hi type="italic">paiti</hi> = πρός, and <hi type="italic">gâm</hi>, to go, properly, “the going to,” therefore <hi type="italic">message, edict</hi>, then generally <hi type="italic">word</hi> (as here) and <hi type="italic">matter</hi> (Ezr 6:11), as frequently in the Targ., corresponding to the Hebr. דּבר.
entries.29fcd5d67d7619eee1a550f761ba49dcb793b44b: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.17-Dan.3.18">Dan 3:17-18</reference> יכיל denotes the <hi type="italic">ethical ability</hi>, i.e., the ability limited by the divine holiness and righteousness, not the omnipotence of God as such. For this the accused did not doubt, nor will they place in question the divine omnipotence before the heathen king. The conclusion begins after the Athnach, and הן means, not <hi type="italic">see! lo!</hi> (according to the old versions and many interpreters), for which Daniel constantly uses אלוּ or ארו, but it means <hi type="italic">if</hi>, as here the contrast לא והן, <hi type="italic">and if not</hi> (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.18">Dan 3:18</reference>), demands. There lies in the answer, “If our God will save us, then ... and if not, know, O king, that we will not serve thy gods,” neither audacity, nor a superstitious expectation of some miracle (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.17">Dan 3:17</reference>), nor fanaticism (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.18">Dan 3:18</reference>), as Berth., v. Leng., and Hitz. maintain, but only the confidence of faith and a humble submission to the will of God. “The three simply see that their standpoint and that of the king are altogether different, also that their standpoint can never be clearly understood by Nebuchadnezzar, and therefore they give up any attempt to justify themselves. But that which was demanded of them they could not do, because it would have been altogether contrary to their faith and their conscience. And then without fanaticism they calmly decline to answer, and only say, 'Let him do according to his own will;' thus without superstitiousness committing their deliverance to God” (Klief.).
entries.ceccaf3447d55a6600268208b5200ec813d4540a: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.19-Dan.3.20">Dan 3:19-20</reference> <hi type="italic">The judgment pronounced on the accused, their punishment, and their miraculous deliverance</hi>. <div eID="gen15559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15560" type="x-p"/> After the decided refusal of the accused to worship his gods, Nebuchadnezzar changed his countenance toward them. Full of anger at such obstinacy, he commanded that the furnace should be heated seven times greater than was usual (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.19">Dan 3:19</reference>), and that the rebels should be bound in their clothes by powerful men of his army, and then cast into the furnace (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.20">Dan 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.21">Dan 3:21</reference>). The form of his countenance changed, and his wrath showed itself in the lineaments of his face. The <hi type="italic">Kethiv</hi> אשׁתּנּו (<hi type="italic">plur</hi>.) refers to the genitive [אנפּוהי, plur., “of his countenances”] as the chief idea, and is not, after the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, to be changed into the <hi type="italic">sing</hi>. למזא for למאזא. On הד־שׁבעה, <hi type="italic">sevenfold</hi>, cf. Winer, <hi type="italic">Chald. Gram.</hi> §59, 5. חזה דּי על, <hi type="italic">beyond that which was fit</hi>, i.e., which was necessary. Seven is used as expressive of an exceedingly great number, with reference to the religious meaning of the punishment.
entries.65f3b8c7557d8c04cb1bceedaa739ea0a2b41a88: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.21">Dan 3:21</reference> <div eID="gen15560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15561" type="x-p"/> Of the different parts of clothing named, סרבּלין are not hose, short stockings, from which Hitz. concludes that the enumeration proceeds from the inner to the outer clothing. This remark, correct in itself, proves nothing as to the covering for the legs. This meaning is given to the word only from the New Persian <hi type="italic">shalwa</hi>̂r, which in the Arabic is <hi type="italic">sara</hi>̂wîl; cf. Haug in Ew.'s <hi type="italic">bibl. Jahrbb</hi>. v. p. 162. But the word corresponds with the genuine Semitic word <hi type="italic">sirbal</hi>, which means <hi type="italic">tunica</hi> or <hi type="italic">indusium</hi>; cf. Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>.<note placement="foot">The lxx have omitted סרבּלין in their translation. Theodot. has rendered it by σαράβαρα, and the third-named piece of dress כּרבּלן by περικνημῖδες, which the lxx have rendered by τιάρας ἐπὶ τῶν κεφαλῶν. Theodoret explains it: περικνημῖδας δὲ τὰς καλουμένας ἀναξυρίδας λέγει. These are, according to Herod. vii. 161, the αναχυρίδες, i.e., <hi type="italic">braccae</hi>, worn by the Persians περὶ τὰ σκέλεα. Regarding Σαράβαρα Theodoret remarks: ἔστι Περσικῶν περιβολαίων εἴδη. Thus Theodot. and Theodor. expressly distinguish the σαράβαρα (סרבּלין) from the περικνημῖδες; but the false interpretation of סרבּלין by <hi type="italic">breeches</hi> has given rise to the confounding of that word with כּרבּלן, and the identification of the two, the περικνημῖδες being interpreted of <hi type="italic">covering for the feet</hi>; and the Vulg. translates the passage: “<hi type="italic">cum braccis suis et tiaris et calceamentis et vestibus</hi>,” while Luther has “cloaks, shoes, and hats.” This confounding of the two words was authorized by the Greek scholiasts, to which the admission of the Persian <hi type="italic">shalwâr</hi> into the Arabic <hi type="italic">saravilu</hi> may have contributed. In Suidas we find the right interpretation along with the false one when he says: Σαράβαρα ἐσθὴς Περσικὴ ἔνιοι δὲ λέγουσι βρακία. Hesychius, on the other hand, briefly explains σαράβαρα by βρακία, κνημῖδες, σκελέαι. Hence the word in the forms <hi type="italic">sarabara, siravara, saravara </hi>or<hi type="italic">saraballa, sarabela</hi>, is commonly used in the middle ages for <hi type="italic">hose</hi>, and has been transferred into various modern languages; cf. Gesen. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 971.</note> p. 970, and <hi type="italic">Heb. Lex. s. v.</hi> Accordingly, סרבּלין denotes <hi type="italic">under-clothing</hi> which would be worn next the body as our shirt. פּטישׁיהון, for which the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> uses the form פּטשׁיהון, corresponding to the Syriac petš<hi type="italic">ayhūn</hi>, is explained in the Hebr. translation of the Chald. portions of Daniel by כּתנת, <hi type="italic">tunica</hi>, and is derived from פשׁט, <hi type="italic">expandit</hi> (by the transposition of the second and third radicals). Thus the Syriac word is explained by Syr. lexicographers. Theodotion’s translation, τιάραι, is probably only hit upon from the similarity of the sound of the Greek πέτασος, <hi type="italic">the covering for the head</hi> worn by the ἔφηβοι. כּרבּלן are <hi type="italic">mantles</hi>, from כּרבּל, R. כּבל, <hi type="italic">to bind, to lay around</hi>, with <hi type="italic">r</hi> intercalated, which occurs <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.27">1Ch 15:27</reference> of the putting around or putting on of the מעיל (upper garment). לבוּשׁיהון are <hi type="italic">the other pieces of clothing</hi> (Aben Ezra and others), not <hi type="italic">mantles</hi>. For that לבוּשׁ was specially used of over-clothes (Hitz.) cannot be proved from <reference osisRef="Job.24.7">Job 24:7</reference> and 2Ki 10:22. We have here, then, the threefold clothing which, according to Herodotus, i. 195, the Babylonians wore, namely, the סרבּלין, the κιθῶν ποδηνεκὴς λίνεος, the פּטישׁא worn above it, ἄλλον εἰρίνεον κιθῶνα, and the כּרבּלא thrown above that, χλανίδιον λευκόν; while under the word לבוּשׁיהון the other articles of clothing, coverings for the feet and the head, are to be understood.<note placement="foot">With the setting aside of the false interpretation we have disposed of the objection against the historical character of the narrative which v. Leng. and Hitz. have founded on the statement of Herodotus <hi type="italic">l.c.</hi>, that the Babylonians wore no hose, but that they were first worn by the Persians, who adopted them from the Medes.</note> <div eID="gen15561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15562" type="x-p"/> The separate articles of clothing, consisting of easily inflammable material, are doubtlessly mentioned with reference to the miracle that followed, that even these remained unchanged (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.27">Dan 3:27</reference>) in the fiery furnace. In the easily inflammable nature of these materials, namely, of the fine κιθῶν ποδηνεκὴς λίνεος, we have perhaps to seek the reason on account of which the accused were bound in their clothes, and not, as Theodoret and most others think, in the haste with which the sentence against them was carried out.
entries.9c59edffa42b9c40cf43d94877c4d584f54b6cec: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.22-Dan.3.23">Dan 3:22-23</reference> דּי מן (<hi type="italic">because that</hi>), a further explanatory expression added to דּנה כּל־קבל (<hi type="italic">wholly for this cause</hi>): because the word of the king was sharp, and in consequence of it (ו), the furnace was heated beyond measure for that reason. The words אלּך גּבריּא (<hi type="italic">these mighty men</hi>) stand here in the <hi type="italic">status absol.</hi>, and are again taken up in the pronoun המּון after the verb קטּל. If the three were brought up to the furnace, it must have had a mouth above, through which the victims could be cast into it. When heated to an ordinary degree, this could be done without danger to the men who performed this service; but in the present case the heat of the fire was so great, that the servants themselves perished by it. This circumstance also is mentioned to show the greatness of the miracle by which the three were preserved unhurt in the midst of the furnace. The same thing is intended by the repetition of the word מכפּתין, <hi type="italic">bound</hi>, <reference osisRef="Dan.3.23">Dan 3:23</reference>, which, moreover, is purposely placed at the close of the passage to prepare for the contrast שׁרין, <hi type="italic">at liberty</hi>, free from the bonds, Dan 3:25.<note placement="foot">Between <reference osisRef="Dan.3.23">Dan 3:23</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.3.24">Dan 3:24</reference> the lxx have introduced the Prayer of Azariah and the Song of the three men in the fiery furnace; and these two hymns are connected together by a narrative which explains the death of the Chaldeans who threw the three into the furnace, and the miracle of the deliverance of Daniel’s friends. Regarding the apocryphal origin of these additions, composed in the Greek language, which Luther in his translation has rightly placed in the Apocrypha, see my <hi type="italic">Lehr. der Einl. in d. A. Test</hi>. §251.</note>
entries.c520361f06e6687c145a2f758cb21cdfd99f3e0f: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.24-Dan.3.27">Dan 3:24-27</reference> <div eID="gen15562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15563" type="x-p"/> The king, who sat watching the issue of the matter, looked through the door into the furnace, and observed that the three who had been cast into it bound, walked about freed from their bonds and unhurt; and, in truth, he saw not the three only, but also a fourth, “like to a son of the gods,” beside them. At this sight he was astonished and terrified. He hastily stood up; and having assured himself by a consultation with his counsellors that three men had indeed been cast bound into the furnace, while he saw four walking in the midst of it, he approached the mouth of the furnace and cried to the three to come forth. They immediately came out, and were inspected by the assembled officers of state, and found to be wholly uninjured as to their bodies, their clothes being unharmed also, and without even the smell of fire upon them. הדּברין refers, without doubt, to the officers of the kingdom, <hi type="italic">ministers</hi> or <hi type="italic">counselors of state</hi> standing very near the king, since they are named in <reference osisRef="Dan.3.27">Dan 3:27</reference> and <reference osisRef="Dan.6.8">Daniel 6:8</reference> (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.7">Dan 6:7</reference>) along with the first three ranks of officers, and (<reference osisRef="Dan.4.23">Dan 4:23</reference> [26]) during Nebuchadnezzar’s madness they conducted the affairs of government. The literal meaning of the word, however, is not quite obvious. Its derivation from the Chald. דּברין, <hi type="italic">duces</hi>, with the Hebr. article (Gesen.), which can only be supported by מדברא, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.14">Pro 11:14</reference> (Targ.), is decidedly opposed by the absence of all analogies of the blending into one word of the article with a noun in the Semitic language. The <hi type="italic">Alkoran</hi> offers no corresponding analogues, since this word with the article is found only in the more modern dialects. But the meaning which P. v. Bohlen (<hi type="italic">Symbolae ad interp. s. Codicis ex ling. pers.</hi> p. 26) has sought from the Persian word which is translated by <hi type="italic">simul judex, </hi>i.e.,<hi type="italic">socius in judicio</hi>, is opposed not only by the fact that the compensation of the <hi type="italic">Mim</hi> by the Dagesch, but also the composition and the meaning, has very little probability. <div eID="gen15563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15564" type="x-p"/> The fourth whom Nebuchadnezzar saw in the furnace was like in his appearance, i.e., as commanding veneration, to a son of the gods, i.e., to one of the race of the gods. In <reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">Dan 3:28</reference> the same personage is called an angel of God, Nebuchadnezzar there following the religious conceptions of the Jews, in consequence of the conversation which no doubt he had with the three who were saved. Here, on the other hand, he speaks in the spirit and meaning of the Babylonian doctrine of the gods, according to the theogonic representation of the συζυγία of the gods peculiar to all Oriental religions, whose existence among the Babylonians the female divinity Mylitta associated with Bel places beyond a doubt; cf. Hgst. <hi type="italic">Beitr</hi>. i. p. 159, and Häv., Kran., and Klief. <hi type="italic">in loc.</hi> <div eID="gen15564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15565" type="x-p"/> Acting on this assumption, which did not call in question the deliverance of the accused by the miraculous interposition of the Deity, Nebuchadnezzar approached the door of the furnace and cried to the three men to come out, addressing them as the servants (worshippers) of the most high God. This address does not go beyond the circle of heathen ideas. He does not call the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego the only true God, but only the most high God, the chief of the gods, just as the Greeks called their Zeus ὁ ὕψιστος θεός. The <hi type="italic">Kethiv</hi> עלּיא (in Syr. <hi type="italic">̀elāyā̀</hi>, to preserve) is here and everywhere in Daniel (v. 32; <reference osisRef="Dan.4.14">Dan 4:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.21">Dan 4:21</reference>, etc.) pointed by the Masoretes according to the form עילאה (with )ה prevailing in the Targg. The forms גשׁם, גּשׁמא, are peculiar to Daniel (v. 27f., <reference osisRef="Dan.4.30">Dan 4:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.5.21">Dan 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.11">Dan 7:11</reference>). The Targg. have גּוּשׁמא instead of it.
entries.491b712558a30bd0d563dcb31e7af8f03a0984aa: <reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">Dan 3:28</reference> <hi type="italic">The impression made by this event on Nebuchadnezzar.</hi> <div eID="gen15565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15566" type="x-p"/> The marvellous deliverance of the three from the flames of the furnace produced such an impression on Nebuchadnezzar, that he changed his earlier and humbler judgment (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.15">Dan 3:15</reference>) regarding the God of the Jews, and spoke now in praise of the might of this God. For at the same time he not only openly announced that He had saved (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.28">Dan 3:28</reference>) His servants, but also by an edict, issued to all the peoples of his kingdom, he forbade on pain of death the doing of any dishonour to the God of the Jews (<reference osisRef="Dan.3.29">Dan 3:29</reference>). Nebuchadnezzar, however, did not turn to the true God. He neither acknowledged Jehovah as the only, or the alone true God, nor did he command Him to be worshipped. He only declared Him to be a God who is able to save His servants as no other could, and merely forbade the despising and reviling of this God. Whoever speaks שׁלה, <hi type="italic">that which is erroneous</hi> or unjust, against the God of Shadrach, etc., shall be put to death. שׁלה, from שׁלה, <hi type="italic">to err, to commit a fault</hi>, is changed in the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> into שׁלוּ, which occurs in <reference osisRef="Dan.6.5">Dan 6:5</reference> and Ezr 4:22, and in the Targg.; but without sufficient ground, since with other words both forms are found together, e.g., ארמלא, <hi type="italic">vidua</hi>, with ארמלוּ, <hi type="italic">viduitas</hi>. According to this, שׁלוּ <hi type="italic">in abstr.</hi> means the <hi type="italic">error</hi>; שׁלה <hi type="italic">in concr</hi>., <hi type="italic">the erroneous</hi>. Hitz. finds the command partly too narrow, partly quite unsuitable, because an error, a simple oversight, should find pardon as soon as possible. But the distinction between a fault arising from mistake and one arising from a bad intention does not accord with the edict of an Oriental despot, which must be in decided terms, so that there may be no room in cases of transgression for an appeal to a mere oversight.
